Can the way gains combine predict how recursive systems scale?

Theory The Foundational Paper of the ARC Theory, within Recursive Dynamics: the foundation of Law I, the ARC Principle, a law under test

Michael Darius Eastwood

Independent Researcher, London, United Kingdom
ORCID 0009-0004-3222-7442 michael@michaeldariuseastwood.com

The Foundational Paper of the ARC Theory, within Recursive Dynamics: the cross-domain foundation of Law I, the ARC Principle, and the formalism of the growth exponent that Law III, the ARC Ceiling, caps, each a law under test; it states the ARC Bound as the theory registration holds it, a ceiling of at most two for correctors of the system’s own class, whose point value two is a conjecture, and it bears on Law V, the ARC Embedding Law (added on 24 September 2026 and registered as a law on 15 October 2026 in version 1.103 of that registration, a law under test, the registered result on its placement limb given in Section 8; its mathematics in development), through the conditional prediction of Section 6.5, beside which it reports a pilot of the Eden Protocol. Abstract

I believe advanced AI is an existential risk unless values and correction are built into how it reasons; only proof will move the world. Predicting how a system improves requires separating a mathematical model from evidence that the system follows it. This cross-domain foundation of the ARC Theory asks whether the way gains combine can predict later scaling. Specified continuous functional equations restrict scaling families; associativity of an update rule alone does not. A cumulative-advantage model gives the shifted power law g(r)=[1+(1−βL)ar]1/(1−βL)g(r)=[1+(1-\beta_L)ar]^{1/(1-\beta_L)}, with asymptotic exponent α=1/(1−βL)\alpha=1/(1-\beta_L). Its characteristic scale requires a declared depth coordinate and an operational crossover criterion. Fixed model weights and fixed update rules imply no universal capability exponent. Biological and physical comparisons are separated into measurements, analytic references and analogies; the proposed general dimensional bridge remains unproved. The one interpretable AI error-suppression fit is inconclusive and does not identify a capability-growth exponent. A registered pilot supports its pooled performance contrast under the registered scoring rule, with engine dependence, a disclosed recovery amendment and a mechanism test that was not evaluable; it validates none of the exponent, crossover or ceiling claims. The ARC Ceiling remains a law under test with conditional premises, not a universal safety guarantee. The decisive next test is prospective: classify composition independently, lock the scaling prediction, and compare held-out trajectories with serious rival models. The contribution is a framework for predictions that can fail, with each mathematical and empirical claim kept at its demonstrated scope.

Version 5.22, revised 1 November 2026, distinguishes error suppression from capability growth and a characteristic depth from elasticity crossing one, and retains superseded claims in Appendix B.

1 Introduction

I believe advanced AI is an existential risk unless values and correction are built into how it reasons; only proof will move the world. If control of a capable AI system were lost and could not be won back, what the system itself carries would decide what it does. People should keep oversight, containment and shutdown for as long as they physically can, and never surrender them by choice. Embedded correction is the programme’s contingency for control lost against our will. Testing that ambition requires knowing what improves, on which axis, and under which constraints.

This paper develops one part of that foundation: can the way a system combines gains predict how its later performance scales? It compares computational, biological and physical examples, while distinguishing model assumptions from observations. A useful answer would let a researcher make a prediction before seeing the full curve, and identify where that prediction fails. No exponent derived here establishes that a deployed AI system remains safe or correctable.

This paper belongs to the ARC Theory, the founding theory of Recursive Dynamics, the science of systems that improve themselves, which the author founded (the founding paper). The theory is carried by five laws, each a law under test: Law I, the ARC Principle, that usable capability is a power of recursive depth, with the exponent measured rather than assumed; Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law; Law III, the ARC Ceiling; and Laws IV and V, the ARC Persistence Law and the ARC Embedding Law, added on 24 September 2026, their mathematics in development. The laws and twenty-two propositions are registered on OSF (the theory registration), and the statement paper states the theory whole. The programme’s engineering hypothesis is the Eden Protocol, correction built into a system’s own reasoning, whose pilot Section 6.5 reports; its end goal is to learn, by registered tests, whether correction built into a self-improving system can keep pace with its capability, as the contingency for control lost against our will. This paper brings four fields together, AI reasoning, quantum error correction, acoustic physics and consciousness science, and assumes no reader knows the others: Section 1.1 says what each reported, and Appendix G places the paper among the laws.

The mathematical statements are conditional. Specified functional equations constrain a family; the cumulative-advantage ODE selects an asymptotic exponent under its own assumptions. Neither result proves that a real system satisfies those premises. The structural properties hold in every substrate whose recursion satisfies the axioms and the premises Theorem 4 names, because the axioms name no substrate. The empirical hypothesis is that an independently justified composition description helps predict fresh trajectories better than alternative models. That separates the framework’s mathematical content from the prospective success it still needs to demonstrate.

Our contributions are:

  • A formalism. Three axioms, separability, cumulative advantage and continuity (Section 3.1), and the recursive composition operator ⊕\oplus, which characterises how incremental gains combine with accumulated capability (Definition 1), giving the generalised ARC Equation (2).

  • A classification. Under each case’s hypotheses, multiplicative ⊕\oplus yields power-law scaling (RαR^{\alpha}), additive ⊕\oplus yields exponential scaling (eαre^{\alpha r} in the added passes r=R−1r = R - 1), and bounded ⊕\oplus yields saturation (Theorem 1), with the domain and error conditions of any stability claim stated separately (Section 3.2).

  • The exponent derived, not fitted. Within the stated model, the asymptotic exponent is α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) (Theorem 2); no additive decomposition of capability is consistent with the axioms (Theorem 2a); and the characteristic scale R*=α/aR^* = \alpha/a is independent of base potential only while aa and βL\beta_L remain fixed (Theorem 3).

  • Conditional consequences and limits. The model supplies a characteristic scale, depth dependence and a multiplicative dependence on base quality. A capacity ceiling requires further premises. Changing local estimates in computational examples motivates the transition conjecture but does not prove a physical change of composition class (Theorem 4; Conjecture 5).

  • The ARC Bound, stated as registered. The claim that the ceiling of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, is at most two for correctors of the system’s own class, which needs P6 and P20 and nothing else, with the point value two a conjecture; this paper’s own earlier form of it, the coupling at which the sustained exponent reaches two (βL=0.5\beta_L = 0.5, α=2\alpha = 2), is an early-framework conjecture that decides nothing registered (Section 6.4).

  • Graded evidence and tests. Evidence from four domains (Section 4), thirteen falsification criteria (Section 7), a cross-domain forward prediction (Section 6.1), a measurement protocol (Appendix E) and a computational validation suite checking the core mathematical relationships to machine precision (Appendix F).

The ARC Principle is Law I as the theory registration states it: usable capability is a power of recursive depth, with the exponent measured rather than assumed. The first four items are this paper’s framework for it, and the earlier conjunction claim and its criterion F4 remain recorded with their corrected status in Section 7; Law I takes its word through P1 alone, so no result on F4 refutes Law I. The power law is the form the framework derives for multiplicative composition, and the registration places the cross-domain claims beside Law I, as P9 and P18. The fifth item belongs to Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test.

Section 1.1 sets out the four programmes and the question they raise, and Section 1.2 the ARC Equation and its generalisation. Section 2 places the work among related work, antecedents and the rival instrument. Section 3 gives the formalism: the axioms, the composition operator and Theorems 1 to 4. Section 4 reviews the evidence property by property, Section 5 explains the forms across domains, and Section 6 states the predictions and the ARC Bound as registered. Section 7 lists the falsification criteria, Section 8 says what the paper does and does not show, Section 9 states its limitations, and Section 10 concludes. Appendix A gives the proofs, Appendix B the version history and every correction, Appendix C the priority record, Appendix D the notation, Appendix E the measurement protocol, Appendix F the computational validation suite, and Appendix G the paper’s place in the ARC Theory.

1.1 The problem

Between August 2024 and February 2026, four research programmes reported the following results:

Google Quantum AI (results announced 9 December 2024; the team’s preprint public from 24 August 2024) demonstrated exponential suppression of the logical error rate below the surface-code threshold on the Willow processor, by a factor Λ=2.14±0.02\Lambda = 2.14 \pm 0.02 for each increase of two in code distance (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024), a result graded here as convergent timing, not a prediction.

DeepSeek-AI (preprint January 2025; in Nature, September 2025) showed that “the reasoning abilities of LLMs can be incentivized through pure reinforcement learning (RL)”, with the emergence of reasoning patterns such as self-reflection and verification (Guo et al. 2025). Sharma and Chopra (2025) reported that sequential refinement, in which chains build on previous attempts, outperformed parallel self-consistency at matched compute in 95.6% of configurations, across five open-source models and three reasoning benchmarks. Their paper is dated before the experiment reported here, so it is the earlier demonstration of that advantage and not a confirmation of this work. The direction is also not settled: Gu et al. (2026), posted in April 2026, report the opposite result, parallel sampling outperforming sequential across three model families on mathematics and coding, attributing it to reduced exploration when a chain conditions on its own previous answers.

NYU Physics (February 2026) created a continuous classical time crystal with a pair of acoustically levitated beads: “Unless the particles have identical scattering properties, their wave-mediated interactions are nonreciprocal”, and pairs can use this nonreciprocity “to harvest energy from the wave to sustain steady-state oscillations despite viscous drag and the absence of periodic driving” (Morrell et al. 2026). The oscillation is a linearly stable limit cycle. In one experiment the antisymmetric mode’s coherence time is τ=(100±10)\tau = (100 \pm 10) s, about 6,700 cycles at 66.787 Hz, comparable to the 108 s recording, and the authors add: “Sustained oscillations persist for hours longer than the measurement window, which means that the true coherence time of the nonequilibrium steady state may be substantially larger.” Every recording the paper reports is of a steady state, and no growth exponent has been measured in this system.

The COGITATE Consortium (2025) found information about conscious content in visual, ventrotemporal and inferior frontal cortex, content-specific decoding in posterior regions generalising for about the duration of the stimulus (0.5 to 1.5 s) while in prefrontal regions its temporal generalisation was restricted to about 0.2 to 0.4 s (Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025). COGITATE tested two theories of consciousness, not a recursion depth, and its results challenge key tenets of both; this paper reads the sustained, content-specific posterior responses as structurally consistent with depth-dependent, feedback-driven processing, which COGITATE did not measure.

These programmes address different problems in different physical substrates. They report different things: exponential suppression of error in quantum error correction, a contested sequential advantage in AI reasoning, a sustained steady-state limit cycle in a classical time crystal, and no measured form in neuroscience. They are separate programmes in separate fields.

Yet, on this paper’s reading, they share a structural pattern: in each, recursive or recurrent processing (where the output of one cycle becomes the input for the next), operating on structured asymmetry, is what the reported gain or order depends on. Those programmes are cited for convergence and not for mechanism: whether any of their systems accumulates, meaning retains something from each pass whose contribution grows with depth, rather than merely conditioning on the previous pass, is untested in each case. The question this paper addresses is whether that pattern reflects a single underlying principle or mere coincidence.

1.2 The ARC Equation

We formalise the question as follows. For AI systems, the equation is U=I×Rα,\begin{equation*} U = I \times R^{\alpha} , \end{equation*}(1) the ARC Equation (AI power-law form). Separately, the ARC Bound is the registration’s claim that the ceiling of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, is at most two for correctors of the system’s own class; Paper X supersedes this fixed-exponent framing as the operative safety criterion and re-scopes, without retracting, the equation and the bound (Section 6.4). Here α\alpha is the exponent of the declared capability observable; the error-suppression fit reported below is a different estimand (Section 3.1). The two is not a property of the equation: it is the value Law III’s ceiling, 1/(1−γ)1/(1-\gamma), returns where the correction-leverage exponent γ\gamma is one half, a point value the registration conjectures and does not assert (Section 6.4). Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, a law under test, is stated as the registration states it, βC>k\beta_C > k: correction has the asymptotic scaling advantage where its exponent exceeds the drift exponent, burden has it where the correction exponent is the smaller, and at equality coefficients, delay, backlog and saturation decide the outcome. In Paper X’s minimal model, with positive gain drift, βC>k\beta_C > k decides whether the misalignment fraction vanishes, and with level drift as well the condition is βC>max⁡(k,0)\beta_C > \max(k, 0).

Here UU denotes effective capability (the letter’s earlier senses in this programme are recorded in Appendix D.1), II denotes base potential (structured asymmetry; the notation register’s base intelligence, what the system could do before any self-improvement), RR denotes recursive depth, and α\alpha denotes the scaling exponent. Within the stated model this paper derives α\alpha rather than fitting it: the asymptotic exponent follows from the self-referential coupling βL\beta_L via α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L). That the exponent is bounded by two is not a result of this model: it belongs to Law III, and Section 6.4 states it as the registration does, a claim on the correction-leverage exponent and not on the coupling. In the v5 cross-architecture experiment of Paper II, the one interpretable sequential error-suppression fit, on Gemini 3 Flash, is inconclusive (Section 4.3). The reported sequential advantage applies where both error exponents could be estimated; the original super-linear error-suppression forecast was not borne out. These observations supply no measurement of βL\beta_L or of a universal capability-growth regime.

But this power-law form is itself a special case. Define the recursive composition operator ⊕\oplus, which characterises how incremental gains combine with accumulated capability. When a justified model of composition induces one of the specified functional equations on the observable, continuity restricts its scaling family; it does not select the exponent from associativity alone: U(R)=I×f⊕(R,βL),\begin{equation*} U(R) = I \times f_{\oplus}(R, \beta_L) , \end{equation*}(2) the generalised ARC Equation. Under the regularity and composition hypotheses of Theorem 1: multiplicative ⊕\oplus yields power-law scaling (RαR^{\alpha}), additive ⊕\oplus yields exponential scaling (eαre^{\alpha r} in the added passes r=R−1r = R - 1), and bounded ⊕\oplus yields saturation.

2 Related work, antecedents and the rival instrument

The formalism rests on mathematics far older than this programme, and much of its cross-domain evidence is other researchers’ work, beside the programme’s own experiment, comparisons and pilot (Sections 4.3, 6.1 and 6.5); this section states each debt in the source’s own terms and then weighs the nearest work.

Exact equations, asymptotic scaling and noisy observations.

Cauchy’s functional equations supply the exact families (Cauchy 1821); stability results impose their own domain and error assumptions (Hyers 1941; Baker et al. 1979). Regular variation is an established setting for asymptotic behaviour near powers (Bingham et al. 1987); Bingham and Ostaszewski (2015) connect Cauchy and related functional equations with asymptotic limits under explicit side conditions. These results motivate separating an exact identity from an asymptotic approximation and an empirical fit. None establishes a universal scaling form for arbitrary recursive updates.

Fitting is part of the hypothesis.

Xiao et al. (2011) show why the observation-error model matters when choosing between log-transformed regression and nonlinear regression. Model comparisons must refer to the same measured response with comparable likelihoods. Appendix E therefore requires the error model, diagnostics and uncertainty procedure to be specified before selecting a scaling family.

The dimensional formula.

The physical models discussed in Section 6.4 have different observables and premises (West et al. 1997, 2004; Banavar et al. 1999, 2010; Demetrius 2008; Demetrius and Tuszynski 2010; Zhao 2022; Bettencourt 2013). The conditional transport result identifies when d/(d+1)d/(d+1) follows for delivery against flow-length cost; a general common derivation for metabolic, urban and other exponents remains unproved. Neither that formula nor the classical Cauchy families are claimed as new.

The forms, conceded.

The relation α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) of Theorem 2 is the exponent of the elementary solution of the separable equation Axiom 2 states. The same structure, a stock that grows at a rate proportional to a power below one of itself, is the knowledge production function of Jones (1995), whose long-run growth rate carries the factor 1/(1−ϕ)1/(1-\phi); the expression 1/(1−βL)1/(1-\beta_L) is also the sum of a geometric series, familiar as the Keynes multiplier (Keynes 1936) and as Dyson resummation (Dyson 1949), as Paper X’s novelty ledger records of this paper. Axiom 2’s name, cumulative advantage, is the term of Price (1976). What this paper adds is not these forms but the axioms that select among them and their reading across domains.

The four programmes and their neighbours.

The programmes of Section 1.1 are cited for convergence, not mechanism. A photonic metamaterial analogue of a continuous time crystal (Liu et al. 2023) and a continuous space-time crystal state driven by nonreciprocal optical forces (Raskatla et al. 2024) have also been reported; recurrent processing as a basis of consciousness has its own literature (Lamme 2006; Zheng et al. 2025); and the scaling of test-time compute in language models has been studied directly (Snell et al. 2024; Zeng et al. 2025; Li et al. 2025).

The pipes premise, with its contest.

The premise that transport networks set the pace of biological growth is not this programme’s claim to defend; it is the premise of a leading account in quantitative biology, and a contested one. West, Brown and Enquist derived the allometric scaling laws of biology from the geometry of nutrient-distribution networks (West et al. 1997; one of the most cited papers in its field, with an OpenAlex citation count of 5,046 as of 12 August 2026, a single-source and index-dependent count). The exact exponent remains contested: White and Seymour report basal metabolic rate proportional to body mass to the two-thirds power rather than three-quarters (White and Seymour 2003), and Kozłowski and Konarzewski have twice asked whether the model is “mathematically correct and biologically relevant” (Kozłowski and Konarzewski 2004, 2005). This programme’s premise needs only the mechanism, that the delivery network sets the ceiling, and not any particular exponent; the dispute over the exponent’s value leaves it untouched, but the critics question the mechanism too, so the programme takes it as a premise, and its biological reading stands or falls with it.

The exception West’s own group found.

The escape from the pipe limit is also not this programme’s assertion; it is measured in the urban scaling literature by the same senior author. Bettencourt et al. (2007) report, in the paper’s own words (their β\beta is a city-scaling exponent, not this paper’s coupling βL\beta_L): “Quantities reflecting wealth creation and innovation have β≈1.2>1\beta\approx1.2>1 (increasing returns), whereas those accounting for infrastructure display β≈0.8<1\beta\approx0.8<1 (economies of scale).” Infrastructure, the literal pipes, scales sublinearly; information-mediated activity scales superlinearly. They state the contrast with biology directly: “we discuss how cities are similar to, and differ from, biological organisms, for which β<1\beta<1”. They derive “growth equations, which quantify the dramatic difference between growth fueled by innovation versus that driven by economies of scale” (spelling as in the original). And their closing inference names the consequence: “This difference suggests that, as population grows, major innovation cycles must be generated at a continually accelerating rate to sustain growth and avoid stagnation or collapse.” On this paper’s reading, that is the shape of the open problem this framework addresses: in the findings of West’s group, information-mediated growth escapes the throughput limit, and the only brake in their framework is external and must be applied again and again, faster and faster. No internal limit is derived. The replacement limit, a ceiling belonging to the growing system itself, is the gap.

The pipes argument at fixed throughput.

Everything that grows is fed through a channel, and for everything before software, fixing the channel fixes the growth. Starve a tumour’s blood supply and its growth is held back. Fix a chain reaction’s fuel and geometry and it stops. Exhaust an epidemic’s susceptible hosts and it burns out. Astrophysics has a named, quantitative constraint of the same kind: the Eddington limit, a luminosity ceiling where radiation pressure balances gravity, not a hard ceiling on accretion, since ultraluminous X-ray sources sit well above it (Bachetti et al. 2014). The claim here is a generalisation of limits physics already accepts, not a new species of assertion. Two hard cases are handled deliberately. Cosmic inflation is excluded by scope: it is expansion of space, not growth of a structure on a substrate, and it ended by field dynamics rather than by running out of anything. Evolution is the sharpest case and it fits: biological complexity increased for billions of years at roughly fixed solar throughput, which is growth on information at fixed pipes, and it is also glacial, and it has no internal corrector at all, since selection is external. On this framework, evolution would carry a measurable exponent far below the ceiling; that is a hypothesis about biology falling out of a framework built for software, stated without a criterion or a planned test, and it lies outside the theory registration’s scope, which places biological systems among those “for which the framework offers an analogy and no measurement”. The physicist’s form of the objection is Landauer’s: computation is physically implemented, so software has pipes too. The fixed-substrate clock is the answer and appears beside the claim: the regime under study holds the physical substrate fixed and asks what still grows, which is why exogenous speed-ups are excluded by definition. The functional form of capability growth in recursive depth remains an empirical question, and the registered analysis does not assume the family: under P1 the power law is compared with its registered rivals, “the logarithmic form, the exponential form, a saturating form, a broken or piecewise power law with one change of regime, and the shifted finite-window solution of this framework’s own growth equation”, and a declining outcome is admissible.

The rival instrument.

The nearest work to this programme’s question, and the right paper to weigh it against, is Engels et al. (2025), first posted 25 April 2025. It asks how oversight itself scales and answers quantitatively: oversight success is modelled as a game between capability-mismatched players whose oversight-specific Elo is a piecewise-linear function of general intelligence with two plateaus, and optimal numbers of oversight levels are derived for Nested Scalable Oversight, in which trusted models oversee stronger untrusted models that then become the trusted models at the next step. The instrument is the difference. Their variable is the capability gap between overseer and overseen, measured in Elo. This programme’s variable is the composition class of the corrector, measured through the corrector’s own scaling exponent. They also state the design condition in slope form: oversight improves with capability when the overseer’s game-specific Elo rises faster with general Elo than the overseen system’s (mG>mHm_G > m_H), and they recommend iterating an oversight design until it does. Their framework has no term for what the overseer is made of, and this paper’s formalism has none either. The programme’s separate prediction, outside this paper’s model, is that iterated same-class oversight, of which Nested Scalable Oversight is an instance, stays capped however many rungs are added, while a cross-class corrector is not held to that cap. The theory registration’s P6 states the cap for same-class correctors, at or below one half, as a conjecture on the correction-leverage exponent of Law III (the ARC Ceiling, a law under test), an exponent the registration keeps distinct from Law II’s βC\beta_C. That is where the two programmes could disagree about a measurable quantity, and this paper does not decide it.

Antecedents and near-misses, each with its differential.

On the question: Hutter asked directly whether intelligence can explode (Hutter 2012, arXiv, 28 February 2012), undertaking to separate speed from intelligence explosion and to consider possible bounds on intelligence, augmenting the analysis of Chalmers (2010); the question itself goes back to Good (1966). What that literature does not contain is a derived ceiling with an architecture dependence; growth exponents of the form used here are older, as this section has conceded. On impossibility: three 2025 arXiv papers argue for limits on alignment or its control (Yao 2025b, public by 13 June 2025, attested by arXiv and independently observed by the Internet Archive; Yao 2025a, 3 July 2025; and Ball et al. 2025, 9 July 2025). All three are worst-case and qualitative: measure zero, coNP-completeness, cryptographic hardness. Their measured object is verification of a fixed system, and it is closed within its own terms; this programme’s measured object is a different one, persistence of alignment as capability compounds under recursive amplification, and closure of the first does not settle the second. None reports an average-case scaling exponent or a rate. The third concludes that “safety cannot be achieved by designing filters external to the LLM internals (architecture and weights)” and argues that “an aligned AI system’s intelligence cannot be separated from its judgment”; that argument from filtering intractability is consistent with this programme’s architecture dependence, though it does not test it. On the mechanism: that anti-correlated estimates average better than independent ones is textbook variance reduction (antithetic variates); the mechanism is not the claim. The claim is that architecture determines whether anti-correlation is available at all, and that this caps a safety-relevant exponent. The nearest structural analogue is the quantum error-correction threshold theorem (Aharonov and Ben-Or 2008), which also converts a qualitative worry into a critical value; it concerns physical error rates in a fixed architecture, not a corrector’s scaling exponent, so it is a near-miss rather than an occupant, and the analogy was identified by this programme’s own search rather than by a referee. On feedback and stability, the general proposition that inadequate corrective gain relative to system gain causes instability has a long control-theory lineage (small-gain theorems; Zames 1966); those are gain conditions on interconnected systems, not a power-law exponent criterion on a corrector’s scaling with the capability of a recursively improving system. The nearest quantitative neighbour is Liu and Meng (2026), which recasts self-correction as a closed-loop control problem via a two-state Markov model and derives a directly measurable stability threshold, iterate only when the error-correction rate over the error-introduction rate exceeds Acc/(1−Acc)\mathrm{Acc}/(1-\mathrm{Acc}). The differential: theirs is a per-step rate threshold at a fixed capability level, deciding whether another iteration helps now; this programme’s criterion is a scaling relation across capability, deciding whether corrective strength keeps pace as the system improves. Theirs has no comparison of correction and drift exponents across capability, the quantities the programme’s co-scaling criterion compares; the two models meet where growth stops, as Paper X shows. Smolin’s cosmological natural selection (Smolin 1992) is the antecedent for selection-shaped universes, and the programme’s own December-era notes cite it contemporaneously.

Feedback, resources and elapsed time.

Cunningham et al. (2026) distinguish algorithmic improvement, capability and aggregate economic effects; feedback elasticities and bottlenecks determine whether a narrow acceleration propagates. This is relevant to the programme’s distinction between recursive depth and elapsed time. It is not a measurement of the correction exponent or a derivation of the ARC Ceiling. Comparing the models requires an explicit mapping of observables, clocks and fixed resources; no equivalence or confirmation is claimed here.

A programme hypothesis beyond the model.

Oversight arrangements that place a human in the loop, as amplification and reinforcement learning from human feedback do, are cross-class by construction, because the human corrector does not share the model’s substrate. The programme therefore hypothesises, beyond what this paper’s equations decide, that human-in-the-loop oversight shows a higher correction exponent than pure-model oversight, for a structural reason rather than a sentimental one. This is testable on existing data and does not require new systems.

3 The formalism

3.1 Three axioms

We begin with three axioms that define the recursive amplification systems this paper treats.

Axiom 1 (Separability). Effective capability decomposes as U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R), where I>0I > 0 is base potential (structured asymmetry; the notation register’s base intelligence), R≥1R \geq 1 is recursive depth, and g(1)=1g(1) = 1 (at depth 1, capability equals base potential).

This axiom asserts that base quality and recursive depth contribute to capability through independent, multiplicative channels. A system with zero base potential (I=0I = 0) achieves zero capability regardless of recursive depth: recursion has nothing to amplify.

Axiom 2 (Cumulative advantage). The amplification factor grows according to accumulated amplification: dgdr=a⋅gβL\frac{dg}{dr} = a \cdot g^{\beta_L}, where the variable r=R−1r = R - 1 tallies the passes taken after the first, so that g=1g = 1 at r=0r = 0 restates Axiom 1’s g(1)=1g(1) = 1 in the added-recursion notation the proofs work in, a>0a > 0 is a rate constant and βL∈[0,1)\beta_L \in [0, 1) is the self-referential coupling parameter.

This axiom specifies a model in which the marginal amplification depends on the current amplification. At βL=0\beta_L=0, its marginal rate is constant and its solution is linear in added depth; this asserts no statistical independence between steps. At βL>0\beta_L>0, the marginal rate increases and the solution is convex, with an asymptotic power exponent above one. Its local elasticity at a finite depth is a separate quantity (Section 6.3). Here βL\beta_L is the elasticity of the stipulated marginal rate with respect to amplification, not automatically a measured fraction of usable context. Separability from base potential requires the rate and coupling parameters to remain fixed when II changes.

Axiom 3 (Continuity). The scaling function gg is continuous and monotonically non-decreasing in RR.

This is a regularity condition. It excludes pathological solutions and ensures measurability.

Choose the observable before the exponent.

Here UU is a specified capability observable, and I=U(1)I=U(1) uses the same units. It is not interchangeable with an error rate or an alignment score. Paper II fits error suppression, E(R)=E0R−αerrE(R)=E_0R^{-\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}}. If E(R)>0E(R)>0 and capability is explicitly defined as the reciprocal-error proxy Cerr(R)=1/E(R)C_{\mathrm{err}}(R)=1/E(R), that exact model gives Cerr(R)/Cerr(1)=RαerrC_{\mathrm{err}}(R)/C_{\mathrm{err}}(1)=R^{\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}}. Accuracy 1−E(R)1-E(R), another task score and an error model with a nonzero floor do not inherit that identity. A finite-window error fit alone identifies neither this paper’s capability exponent nor its ODE coupling βL\beta_L. The independently measured correction exponent βC\beta_C and correction-leverage exponent γ\gamma are different quantities (Section 6.4); Operational Definitions states the metric and model conditions.

3.2 The composition operator

How does the gain from recursive step rr combine with accumulated capability QrQ_r? We formalise this as follows.

Definition 1 (Recursive composition operator). Let ⊕:ℝ+×ℝ+→ℝ+\oplus: \mathbb{R}^+ \times \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+ be the recursive composition operator, defined by Qr+1=Qr⊕δQrQ_{r+1} = Q_r \oplus \delta Q_r, where δQr\delta Q_r is the incremental gain at step rr. The operator ⊕\oplus characterises how incremental gains compose with accumulated capability.

The step-update rule records how a state changes. The functional equations below make a separate claim about how an observable behaves when its input is combined. A derivation or an independently specified measurement procedure must connect the two. Dependence of a marginal gain on the current state alone does not establish that connection.

Theorem 1 (Classification of scaling functions). The following specified equations constrain the scaling function to the families stated below. Their premises include an equation on the observable, not merely associativity of the step-update rule. A boundary value or a separately specified parameter selects a member of a family:

  1. Multiplicative composition (g(R1⋅R2)=g(R1)⋅g(R2)g(R_1 \cdot R_2) = g(R_1) \cdot g(R_2)): under Axioms 1 and 3, the continuous solutions form the family g(R)=Rαg(R)=R^\alpha, with α≥0\alpha\geq0 under monotonicity (power law).

  2. Additive composition (f(r1+r2)=f(r1)⋅f(r2)f(r_1 + r_2) = f(r_1) \cdot f(r_2) in the added passes r=R−1r = R - 1, with f(0)=1f(0) = 1): under Axioms 1 and 3, the continuous solutions form the family f(r)=eαrf(r)=e^{\alpha r}, with α≥0\alpha\geq0 under monotonicity, so g(R)=eα(R−1)g(R)=e^{\alpha(R-1)} and g(1)=1g(1)=1 (exponential).

  3. Bounded composition (Qr+1=min⁡(Qr+δQr,Qmax)Q_{r+1} = \min(Q_r + \delta Q_r,\; Q_{\max})), for 0<Q0≤Qmax0<Q_0\leq Q_{\max} and nonnegative increments: f(R)f(R) is bounded by Qmax/IQ_{\max}/I and converges to a limit no greater than Qmax/IQ_{\max}/I, which it reaches only if the increments sum to at least the remaining gap, equality sufficing for attainment in the limit (saturation). Its ceiling is separable from base potential only if QmaxQ_{\max} is itself proportional to II.

Axiom 2 is not among the premises of cases (1) and (2).

Proof sketch. Cases (1) and (2) follow from the Cauchy functional equations. For (1): let h(x)=ln⁡g(ex)h(x) = \ln g(e^x); then h(x+y)=h(x)+h(y)h(x+y) = h(x) + h(y). Under continuity, h(x)=αxh(x) = \alpha x, giving g(R)=Rαg(R) = R^{\alpha}. For (2): ln⁡f\ln f satisfies ln⁡f(r1+r2)=ln⁡f(r1)+ln⁡f(r2)\ln f(r_1 + r_2) = \ln f(r_1) + \ln f(r_2), a Cauchy additive equation with solution ln⁡f(r)=αr\ln f(r) = \alpha r. Case (3) follows directly from the bound. Full proofs in Appendix A. ◻

The classification settles the behaviour of the specified observable equations and capped recurrence, not of every recursive update rule. Two further classical Cauchy equations are the additive equation h(x+y)=h(x)+h(y)h(x+y)=h(x)+h(y) and the logarithmic equation h(R1R2)=h(R1)+h(R2)h(R_1R_2)=h(R_1)+h(R_2), whose continuous solutions are linear and logarithmic respectively. The observable and its baseline must be stated: the logarithmic equation forces h(1)=0h(1)=0, so it cannot be imposed directly on the amplification gg normalised by g(1)=1g(1)=1. For the baseline-respecting logarithmic rival g(R)=1+clog⁡Rg(R)=1+c\log R, the equation applies to h=g−1h=g-1. Appendix E includes such rivals with their baseline and error assumptions. A given state-update rule must be connected separately to the relevant observable equation. Cases (1) and (2) are Cauchy’s classical results (Cauchy 1821); their conditional validity establishes neither that connection nor an exhaustive classification of recursive systems.

What changes during improvement.

Frozen model weights do not imply a fixed agent. Model parameters, agent code, persistent memory, prompts and tools, and the procedure used to generate subsequent improvements are different objects. An experiment must state which may change, on what schedule, and under what resource allowance. A change in any one of them does not by itself establish faster improvement in the next round.

A fixed update rule does not impose a sub-linear exponent. For example, the unchanged one-dimensional rule F(x)=(x+1)2,x0=1,xn+1=F(xn)F(x)=(\sqrt{x}+1)^2,\qquad x_0=1,\qquad x_{n+1}=F(x_n) gives xn=(n+1)2x_n=(n+1)^2: the initial value has that form, and applying FF to (n+1)2(n+1)^2 gives (n+2)2(n+2)^2. The example is a mathematical counterexample to the general implication, not a model or measurement of an AI system. Conversely, rewriting code need not improve performance. Architectural labels therefore determine neither the sign nor the size of a measured scaling exponent.

The distinction already matters in existing research. The Darwin Gödel Machine revises coding-agent code around frozen pretrained foundation models; its paper separates that implemented scope from future model-training changes (Zhang et al. 2025). AReaL-RSI changes research orientation, stored knowledge and skills across campaigns without updating backbone weights (Zhou et al. 2026). AIDE2^2 reports transferable improvements to research-agent code, while its separate test of the improved agent as the outer-loop improver is inconclusive against its baseline (Srikanth et al. 2026). These are distinct empirical designs, not measurements of this paper’s coupling identity or evidence for a universal exponent.

The hypothesis to test here is narrower: specified changes to an improvement procedure alter subsequent gains under controlled resources. The quantities and the comparison must be fixed before the validation trajectories are observed. In the cumulative-advantage model, a positive βL\beta_L gives an asymptotic exponent above one; whether an implemented agent satisfies that model is an empirical question. Paper II’s single interpretable error-suppression fit remains inconclusive and its earlier super-linear estimate remains retracted. Neither that result nor the architectural distinction settles what future systems can achieve.

Correction and usefulness must be measured together as systems change. Oversight, containment and shutdown remain in human hands for as long as they can be held; embedded correction is a contingency for control lost against our will, not a demonstrated guarantee of later controllability.

Claim-status ladder.

Established mathematics: Cauchy’s equations constrain recursive scaling forms. Empirically grounded: current frontier models are frozen during inference; the Eden pilot found stakeholder-care scores, as its rubric scored them, raised by a prompt-level intervention in all five model runs that could be analysed, under paired tests, a pilot awaiting an independent, preregistered replication. The alignment run of March 2026 is not on this rung: it cannot decide whether alignment scales with depth (Section 6.5).

Hypothesis requiring measurement: changing an agent’s improvement procedure can change its subsequent gains under controlled resources. Neither frozen weights nor self-modification fixes the exponent, and a positive coupling in the model is not an established property of an implemented agent.

Conjectural extrapolation: set out at the close of the paper (Section 10).

The six hidden assumptions.

The stated classification uses the premises of each case. The following modelling choices identify possible extensions. The right-hand columns suggest questions to investigate, not consequences proved by violating a premise:

Table 1. The six hidden assumptions of Theorem 1.
# Assumption Possible extension Example to investigate
1 Continuity Log-periodic oscillations Discrete lattice systems, fractal networks
2 Real-valued Interference and phase Quantum amplitudes, wave mechanics
3 Exact equation Equation-specific error bounds Hyers-Ulam stability (Hyers 1941; Ulam 1960)
4 Single operator Crossover scaling, regime transitions Phase transitions (cf. Conjecture 5)
5 Scalar composition Logarithmic corrections Upper critical dimension
6 Time-independence Dynamic traversal of solution space Adaptive systems, machine learning

Stability is equation-specific. Hyers’ additive result is stated for maps between Banach spaces: a uniform bound on ∥f(x+y)−f(x)−f(y)∥\|f(x+y)-f(x)-f(y)\| for all x,yx,y gives an exact additive map within that bound (Hyers 1941). The exponential result has a different conclusion: a real-valued function on a rational vector space with uniformly bounded residual |f(x+y)−f(x)f(y)||f(x+y)-f(x)f(y)| for all x,yx,y is bounded or satisfies the exponential equation exactly (Baker et al. 1979; Albert and Baker 1982). Neither statement licenses an arbitrary noisy finite sample as evidence for a scaling family. The domain, error norm, regularity and bound must be justified; a small residual on finitely many observed pairs is not a global bound. Nor does a bounded case automatically identify a useful fitted exponential. The earlier claim of stable attractors across the whole function space remains withdrawn.

Assumption 4 is addressed directly by Conjecture 5 (Section 5.5): bounded systems can transition between composition operators as recursive depth increases, which could explain why different studies of the same system can observe different scaling regimes.

From a conditional classification to a prediction.

The exact functional equation restricts a family, and Axiom 2 supplies a separate conditional relation for the asymptotic exponent. Their compatibility on the chosen depth coordinate must also be checked (Section 3.4). Stability theorems do not remove those premises. A useful empirical contribution would be to justify the composition description without knowing the validation curve, seal the resulting prediction, and show that it predicts later observations better than serious alternatives (Section 6.1). No existing fit in this paper establishes that prospective success across domains.

Critical distinction: Cauchy constrains the form, not the exponent.

A persistent misreading of the Cauchy classification is that it predicts a ceiling on recursive scaling. It does not. Cauchy’s functional equations determine that multiplicative composition must produce power-law scaling (g(R)=Rαg(R) = R^\alpha). They say nothing about the value of α\alpha. That value is set by the Bernoulli ODE (α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L)), and as βL→1\beta_L \to 1, α→∞\alpha \to \infty. There is no upper bound internal to the mathematics.

The following table makes the relationship explicit:

Table 2. The exponent α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) at values of the self-referential coupling βL\beta_L.
βL\beta_L (self-referential coupling) α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) Regime
0 1 Linear (no self-reference)
0.5 2 Quadratic
0.75 4 Quartic
0.9 10 Strongly super-linear
0.99 100 Large asymptotic exponent
→1\to 1 →∞\to \infty At fixed depth, g→earg\to e^{ar}

Changing a model’s parameters or update procedure can change its scaling, but no theorem here says that a change of operator causes unbounded growth. The comparison with renormalisation-group ideas (Kadanoff 1966; Wilson 1971) is an analogy about the role of modelling assumptions, not a derivation for AI; version 5.21’s statement of it is kept as Superseded passage 27 (Appendix B.12).

A quadratic ceiling is not a Cauchy result. Law III, the ARC Ceiling, remains a law under test whose value depends on the registered correction premises (Section 6.4). The O(N2)O(N^2) pairwise interactions in full transformer attention count computational interactions in one operation. That count does not bound task capability against recursive depth and provides no derivation of βL=1/2\beta_L=1/2. Frozen and changing architectures must both be measured.

3.3 The βL\beta_L-derivation

For systems satisfying Axiom 2 at fixed parameters, the asymptotic exponent is determined by βL\beta_L. Identifying that parameter independently in an empirical system is a separate requirement.

Theorem 2 (The scaling exponent). Under Axiom 2, at fixed a>0a>0 and 0≤βL<10\leq\beta_L<1, the asymptotic power-law exponent is α=11−βL.\begin{equation*} \alpha = \frac{1}{1 - \beta_L} . \end{equation*}(3)

Proof. Separating variables in dg/dr=agβLdg/dr = a g^{\beta_L}: ∫g−βLdg=∫adr⇒g1−βL1−βL=ar+C.\begin{equation*} \int g^{-\beta_L}\, dg = \int a\, dr \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{g^{1-\beta_L}}{1-\beta_L} = ar + C . \end{equation*}(4) With initial condition g(0)=1g(0) = 1: C=1/(1−βL)C = 1/(1-\beta_L). In the clock Axiom 2 declares, r=R−1r = R - 1: g(r)=[1+(1−βL)ar]1/(1−βL),r≥0,\begin{equation*} g(r) = \left[ 1 + (1-\beta_L)ar \right]^{1/(1-\beta_L)}, \qquad r \geq 0 , \end{equation*}(5) equivalently g(R)=[1+(1−βL)a(R−1)]1/(1−βL)g(R) = \left[ 1 + (1-\beta_L)a(R-1) \right]^{1/(1-\beta_L)} for R≥1R \geq 1. At fixed parameters, as R→∞R\to\infty (so both the unit shift and R*R^* are negligible relative to RR): g(R)≈[(1−βL)aR]1/(1−βL)∝R1/(1−βL).\begin{equation*} g(R) \approx \left[ (1-\beta_L)aR \right]^{1/(1-\beta_L)} \propto R^{1/(1-\beta_L)} . \end{equation*}(6) Therefore α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L). ◻

This derives an asymptotic exponent within Axiom 2. Its empirical test estimates aa and βL\beta_L on disjoint calibration records for the same declared observable, then predicts the complete finite-window trajectory; an asymptotic exponent comparison additionally needs evidence that the asymptotic regime applies. Failure under those fixed conditions rejects this model for that system, whether or not another power law fits. Section 6.1 states the prospective comparison.

Computational check. As a check on the numerics (the identity itself is proved above), the relationship was tested against 30 exact Bernoulli ODE solutions with βL\beta_L values spanning 0.05 to 0.92. The procedure measures βL\beta_L blindly from marginal gains (dg/dRdg/dR vs gg in log-log space, estimated by finite differences of the noiseless closed-form solutions), predicts α\alpha, and compares against the true value; Section 9 reports that numerical derivatives of noisy data bias this estimate. Result: R2=1.00000000R^2 = 1.00000000 (eight decimal places), regression slope =1.000102= 1.000102, mean absolute prediction error =0.002%= 0.002\%. The code is listed under Code and data, after the conclusion.

The multiplicative structure is necessary.

The separable form U=I×f(R,βL)U = I \times f(R, \beta_L) is Axiom 1’s assumption. Theorem 2a makes explicit what that assumption excludes: once Axiom 1 holds and amplification is not trivial, no additive decomposition of capability is possible.

Theorem 2a (Non-additivity). Under Axioms 1 to 3 with βL∈(0,1)\beta_L \in (0, 1), the solution U(I,R)U(I, R) cannot be decomposed as U=f(I)+h(R)U = f(I) + h(R) for any functions ff and hh. The multiplicative interaction is essential.

Proof. Suppose U=f(I)+h(r)U = f(I) + h(r), with depth counted in added passes, r=R−1r = R - 1. By Axiom 1: U=I×g(r)U = I \times g(r) with g(0)=1g(0) = 1. At r=0r = 0 (R=1R = 1): f(I)+h(0)=If(I) + h(0) = I, so f(I)=I−h(0)f(I) = I - h(0). Substituting: I×g(r)=I+[h(r)−h(0)]I \times g(r) = I + [h(r) - h(0)], giving g(r)=1+[h(r)−h(0)]/Ig(r) = 1 + [h(r) - h(0)]/I. Since gg depends only on depth (Axiom 1), but the right side depends on II, we require h(r)=h(0)h(r) = h(0) for all rr, giving g(r)=1g(r) = 1 (no amplification). But Axiom 2 with βL>0\beta_L > 0 guarantees dg/dr=a⋅gβL=a>0dg/dr = a \cdot g^{\beta_L} = a > 0 at r=0r = 0, so gg is non-constant. Contradiction. ◻

This result has a concrete interpretation. A recursive system with zero base quality (I=0I = 0) produces zero capability regardless of depth, and a system at zero added passes (r=0r = 0, the first pass) produces only its base potential, unamplified. Complexity emerges from the interaction between structured input and recursive processing (neither alone is sufficient).

3.4 A characteristic scale and a measurable crossover

For fixed a>0a>0 and 0≤βL<10\leq\beta_L<1, put α=1/(1−βL)\alpha=1/(1-\beta_L) and r=R−1r=R-1. The complete solution is the shifted power law g(r)=(1+rR*)α,R*=αa.g(r)=\left(1+\frac{r}{R^*}\right)^\alpha,\qquad R^*=\frac{\alpha}{a}. Here R*R^* is a scale in added passes, retained under the paper’s existing notation. On the first-pass coordinate its location is R=1+R*R=1+R^*. It is not automatically the onset of super-linear growth.

Theorem 3 (Characteristic scale and local elasticity). Under the stated parameter conditions, at fixed aa and βL\beta_L, g(r)=1+ar+βLa22r2+O(r3)(r→0),g(r)∼(rR*)α(r→∞).g(r)=1+ar+\frac{\beta_La^2}{2}r^2+O(r^3)\quad(r\to0), \qquad g(r)\sim\left(\frac{r}{R^*}\right)^\alpha\quad(r\to\infty). For r>0r>0, the local elasticity in added passes is ηr(r)=dlog⁡gdlog⁡r=αrr+R*.\eta_r(r)=\frac{d\log g}{d\log r}=\frac{\alpha r}{r+R^*}. Thus ηr(R*)=α/2\eta_r(R^*)=\alpha/2. If an operational crossover is defined in advance as attaining a fixed fraction q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1) of the limiting elasticity, it occurs at rq=q1−qR*.r_q=\frac{q}{1-q}R^*. For α>1\alpha>1, local elasticity exceeds one only when r>R*/(α−1)=1/(aβL)r>R^*/(\alpha-1)=1/(a\beta_L). For βL=0\beta_L=0, g(r)=1+arg(r)=1+ar and no super-linear regime occurs.

These are smooth changes, not a discontinuity or a phase transition. In particular, α=1.5\alpha=1.5 gives elasticity 0.750.75 at R*R^*, so naming that scale the onset of super-linearity would be incorrect. The coordinate matters: elasticity measured against R=r+1R=r+1 is αR/(R−1+R*)\alpha R/(R-1+R^*), not ηr\eta_r. The unshifted identity g(R)=Rαg(R)=R^\alpha holds on that coordinate only in the compatible case a=αa=\alpha, or R*=1R^*=1; otherwise the power law is asymptotic.

An empirical test must freeze the observable, the depth origin, the crossover criterion and its tolerance before validation. The choice q=1/2q=1/2 gives an operational meaning to R*R^*; it is a candidate measurement rule, not a retrospective change to a registered criterion. Estimating aa, βL\beta_L and the claimed crossover from the same fitted curve checks algebraic consistency rather than an independent prediction. Predictive evidence requires parameter measurements on disjoint records or a sealed early window, with later trajectories held out.

The expression contains no II when aa and βL\beta_L are held fixed. Invariance under a change of input quality is an additional empirical requirement: input quality may also change either parameter. Nor is this scale unique to recursion; shifted growth curves have characteristic scales in other models. As βL→1\beta_L\to1 at fixed aa and finite rr, g(r)→earg(r)\to e^{ar}. The diverging asymptotic exponent in that limit is not a finite-depth divergence.

3.5 Five derived properties

We now prove that any system satisfying Axioms 1 to 3 with βL>0\beta_L > 0 exhibits five structural properties, two of them on premises Theorem 4 names.

Theorem 4 (Conditional structural consequences). Let a recursive system satisfy Axioms 1 to 3 with βL>0\beta_L > 0. It exhibits the five properties below, each on the premises named with it:

  1. Characteristic scale (Axioms 1 to 3, through Theorem 3). The shifted solution has scale R*=α/aR^*=\alpha/a in added passes. Its local elasticity reaches half its limiting value there; this is a smooth, defined crossover, not a qualitative regime change.

  2. Recursive depth dependence (Axioms 1 and 2). Capability is a strictly increasing function of depth, and convex at every depth: differentiating Axiom 2 gives d2g/dr2=a2βLg2βL−1d^{2}g/dr^{2} = a^{2}\beta_L g^{2\beta_L-1}, which is strictly positive for a>0a > 0 and βL>0\beta_L > 0; R*R^* marks the half-elasticity criterion defined above, not where curvature begins.

  3. Base quality dependence (Axiom 1 alone). UU is proportional to II: capability is zero when I=0I = 0. This follows directly from Axiom 1: U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R).

  4. Multiplicative I×RI \times R interaction. Doubling II doubles UU at any RR (Axiom 1 alone). Doubling RR multiplies UU by 2α2^{\alpha} at any II exactly in the pure-power case, where a=αa = \alpha, and asymptotically otherwise; under bounded composition the doubling law does not hold. The effects compose multiplicatively. This follows from the separable form U=I×g(R)U = I \times g(R).

  5. An external capacity bound, if a further model supplies one. If a specified resource or error mechanism imposes U≤UmaxU\leq U_{\max}, the growing solution cannot continue beyond that bound. Axioms 1 to 3 alone supply no finite UmaxU_{\max}, no saturation depth, and no guarantee of a power-law interval before the bound matters.

Remark 1. At βL=0\beta_L=0 the model is linear in added depth. For βL>0\beta_L>0 it is convex, although a finite-window log-log slope can remain below one; Theorem 3 states the exact local elasticity. The error-suppression fit in Section 4.3 does not measure that capability curvature (Section 3.1). Property 5 has domain-specific analogues: rare correlated errors set a floor near 10−1010^{-10} in high-distance repetition codes (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024), while bounded accuracy limits an AI score. A time crystal has bounded steady-state amplitude, but no growth toward it has been recorded, so it supplies no measured boundary in recursive depth.

The first four statements are consequences of their stated model premises; the fifth requires an additional capacity model. Their occurrence in a physical or computational system is an empirical question. The original five-property conjunction remains part of this paper’s dated history and criterion F4, which decides no registered proposition (Section 1). Correcting its mathematical interpretation does not retrospectively alter a frozen study rule. A future test must specify which premises and which observable consequences it is testing; a conditional identity by itself is not new empirical evidence.

4 Evidence

The record combines different kinds of evidence. An analytic identity establishes a consequence of assumptions. A numerical check on data generated by that identity checks an implementation. A fitted empirical curve describes observations, with its uncertainty and design limits. An analogy proposes a mapping between systems. A prospective test additionally fixes that mapping and a prediction before the validation observations. These categories are kept separate below; a result that fails to reject a value does not establish equivalence to it. In the tables below, a result graded Consistent does not contradict the framework but was not designed to test it, and it is not support.

4.2 Property-by-property evidence

Property 1: threshold behaviour.

Quantum: The surface code threshold pthr≈1%p_{\text{thr}} \approx 1\% is a sharp phase boundary. Above it (p>pthrp > p_{\text{thr}}), a larger code distance makes performance worse. Below it (p<pthrp < p_{\text{thr}}), each increase of two in code distance suppresses the logical error rate by a further factor, so the suppression is exponential in distance. This is the most precisely measured threshold in the evidence base: Google varied physical error rates through controlled error injection and observed the threshold directly (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024).

Physics: The time crystal’s exceptional point (where two eigenvalues of the stability matrix coalesce) marks, on this paper’s reading, the transition from symmetric (bounded) to antisymmetric (compounding) dynamics. Below threshold: active oscillator. At threshold: exceptional point. Above threshold: time crystal (Morrell et al. 2026). The exceptional point is computed from the source’s model; none is measured. Here and throughout this section, the time crystal is a consistency check and a cross-domain analogy, not a test of the framework, and no study of it is registered.

AI: The sequential-over-parallel comparison in Paper II is observed precursor evidence, with one interpretable sequential fit and a second comparison the paper classes as unreliable (Section 4.3). Its arms were not matched in compute. Comparing two procedures does not establish a threshold in a continuously varied parameter.

Property 2: recursive depth dependence.

Quantum: Logical error rate decreases as εd∝Λ−(d+1)/2\varepsilon_d \propto \Lambda^{-(d+1)/2} with code distance dd. Each increase of two in dd enlarges the code’s lattice of physical qubits, and the suppression factor Λ\Lambda applies for each such step (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024); the paper reads code distance as its depth variable by analogy, since the surface code is not a concatenated, recursive code.

AI: Sharma and Chopra (2025) tested seven voting methods for aggregating sequential chain outputs. Methods favouring later reasoning steps (inverse-entropy weighting) achieved optimal performance in 97% of configurations; methods favouring earlier steps achieved optimality in only 17%. This 80-percentage-point gap indicates that later recursive steps carry systematically more information about the correct answer, consistent with capability that compounds with depth (Sharma and Chopra 2025).

Physics: In the source’s linear stability analysis the antisymmetric (breathing) mode grows when the pair lies in its active region, “leading to spontaneous breathing-mode oscillations” (Morrell et al. 2026). Every recording is of a steady state, so that growth has not been observed and no dependence on cycle count has been measured.

Property 3: base quality dependence.

Quantum: Λ=pthr/p\Lambda = p_{\text{thr}}/p depends directly on physical qubit quality (pp). Worse qubits (pp closer to pthrp_{\text{thr}}) give Λ→1\Lambda \to 1 and error correction barely helps. Active leakage removal (DQLR), which maintains qubit quality during operation, improved Λ\Lambda by 35% at distance 5 (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024).

Physics: In the source’s model the pair is active only when the beads differ in size: unless the particles have identical scattering properties their interactions are nonreciprocal, and “The active region vanishes for particles of the same size (a1=a2a_1 = a_2), whose interactions are reciprocal” (Morrell et al. 2026). The framework reads this as an instance of its zero-factor property, a correspondence of structure and not a test.

AI: Base capability I=U(1)I=U(1) must use the declared observable of Section 3.1; accuracy is one possible bounded choice. Proportionality to II is Axiom 1’s assumption at fixed model parameters. No work cited here independently tests that separability across base models.

Property 4: multiplicative I×RI \times R interaction.

Quantum: In the displayed error model, εd∝Λ−(d+1)/2\varepsilon_d\propto\Lambda^{-(d+1)/2}, so ln⁡εd=ln⁡A−d+12ln⁡Λ\ln\varepsilon_d=\ln A-\frac{d+1}{2}\ln\Lambda for a prefactor AA. Increasing Λ\Lambda by a factor qq at fixed AA changes the error rate by q−(d+1)/2q^{-(d+1)/2}, which depends on distance. Quality and distance interact in this model; this does not demonstrate Axiom 1’s separability of II and RR (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024).

AI: In the ARC equation U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha}, base capability and recursive depth are separated multiplicatively by construction (Axiom 1). With one base model, Snell et al. (2024) found that “the effectiveness of different approaches to scaling test-time compute critically varies depending on the difficulty of the prompt”; they did not measure how that benefit varies with the base model’s quality, so a benefit that grows with base quality is this paper’s reading, untested.

Property 5: regime boundaries.

Physics: The time crystal’s oscillation is sustained at bounded amplitude on a linearly stable limit cycle: in the source, higher-order damping can stabilise the growing mode, which then settles into steady-state oscillation (Morrell et al. 2026). Its measured coherence time (Section 1.1) is a property of that steady state, not a ceiling and not a time taken to reach it.

Quantum: In high-distance repetition codes, correlated error bursts create an error floor at approximately 10−1010^{-10} for code distances d≥15d \geq 15, preventing the exponential from continuing indefinitely (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024).

AI: Zeng et al. (2025) found that longer reasoning chains do not consistently improve performance; correct solutions were often shorter than incorrect ones. Longer chains carry more self-revisions, which often degraded performance, and in some models accuracy rose in early revisions and then oscillated. The sequential advantage has boundary conditions (Zeng et al. 2025).

4.3 Contradictory evidence

Several studies challenge the framework’s AI predictions:

Zeng et al. (2025, arXiv:2502.12215) found that for DeepSeek R1, longer chains do not consistently enhance accuracy. Li et al. (2025, arXiv:2502.14382) found that hybrid parallel-sequential approaches outperform pure sequential on code generation. Sharma and Chopra’s (2025) own ablation showed parallel approaches achieve greater semantic diversity on creative tasks while sequential achieves greater lexical diversity, suggesting the sequential advantage applies most strongly to convergent tasks requiring iterative error correction (Sharma and Chopra 2025; Zeng et al. 2025; Li et al. 2025).

These findings limit any general claim of sequential advantage. Restricting a claim after seeing a failure cannot count as an advance prediction of its boundary. A new test must fix its task population, depth range and resource comparison before the outcome is known. Gu et al. (2026) report the opposite direction, parallel sampling outperforming sequential across three model families on mathematics and coding (Section 1.1), so the direction itself is contested.

The error-suppression fits from the capability arm of March 2026.

The v5 experiment of Paper II tested six frontier models on 30 problems with bootstrap confidence intervals; five carried the capability arm, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek R1, Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-5.4 and Groq Qwen3, and Claude Opus 4.6 was measured only in the alignment arm. The five capability runs wrote their records between 11 March 2026 at 15:08 UTC and 12 March 2026 at 04:17 UTC, by the times their own code wrote into each result, and their code and results were first public by GitHub push on 16 March 2026. They are precursor evidence in the theory registration’s sense: they came before it, and they decide no proposition it registers; their two arms were not matched in compute. The fitted quantity is the error-suppression exponent αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} in Section 3.1, against the study’s declared recursive-depth/resource coordinate. One sequential fit is interpretable, Gemini 3 Flash’s, and it is inconclusive: an endpoint estimate of 0.59 with a bootstrap 95 per cent interval of minus 1.3 to 2.9, and a regression estimate of 0.49 with a standard error of 0.20 and a coefficient of determination of 0.86, beside a parallel exponent of 0.31 by endpoint estimate. Paper II classifies the other four runs as near ceiling (Grok 4.1 Fast and DeepSeek R1), a step function (GPT-5.4) and a floor (Groq Qwen3), with no interpretable sequential exponent. It grades the sequential advantage as observed, “Wherever both exponents could be estimated: Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably”, with no parallel exponent for Grok 4.1 Fast, and Gu et al. (2026) report the opposite direction. These fits establish neither super-linear error suppression nor a common error exponent across architectures; they do not measure this paper’s capability-growth exponent or coupling. The update of March 2026 that this section printed, with its table of that month’s estimates, stands in Appendix B.5.

The earlier estimates.

The author’s earlier α\alpha estimates (α≈1.34\alpha \approx 1.34 from n=2n=2 data points; α≈2.2\alpha \approx 2.2 from n=12n=12, 95% CI: 1.5 to 3.0) were preliminary. The later, about 2.2 from twelve problems on one model, is retracted; Paper II gives the reasons for its inflation as twelve problems, one model and a compressed dynamic range. The v5 best fit, Gemini 3 Flash’s (above), is what survived it, one model’s fit and inconclusive, not a correction of the same measurement. No α\alpha has been measured in time crystals. The COGITATE mapping is structural, not quantitative. The neuroscience term ‘recurrent’ and the computational term ‘recursive’ are related but not identical.

5 The composition operator across domains

The following mappings ask whether a domain mechanism justifies one of the specified composition equations. They are proposed explanations whose premises must be checked in each domain.

5.1 AI: multiplicative composition

A later reasoning step can use an earlier answer, but that fact alone establishes neither g(R1R2)=g(R1)g(R2)g(R_1R_2)=g(R_1)g(R_2) nor the cumulative-advantage ODE. The proposed model is that the rate of gain depends on the current amplification by the specified power, at fixed resources and parameters. That is what an independent estimate of βL\beta_L and a held-out trajectory would test.

The βL\beta_L-dynamics equation dg/dr=agβLdg/dr = ag^{\beta_L} models this directly. If βL≈0.5\beta_L \approx 0.5 (moderate coupling), Theorem 2 gives α≈2\alpha \approx 2; the available error-suppression fit is a different estimand (Section 3.1).

Two derivations reach that value and they are not the same derivation, which this paper now states rather than leaves to be noticed. Theorem 2 gives the exponent the coupling sustains, α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1 - \beta_L), where βL\beta_L is the elasticity of marginal amplification in Axiom 2. The ceiling is that of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, αcrit=1/(1−γ)\alpha_{\text{crit}} = 1/(1 - \gamma), and it comes from the correction shortfall rather than from the coupling, where γ\gamma is the correction-leverage exponent (the registration’s letter, written χ\chi in the notation register). Both return two when their exponent is one half; in general they agree exactly where βL=γ\beta_L = \gamma on the same system, which is an open question and is preregistered by timestamp as one (first anchored on 12 August 2026; Appendix C): a drafted study, AG, estimates the coupling and the correction exponent on one and the same system and tests whether the asymptotic growth exponent the coupling sustains respects the ceiling the correction exponent sets (βL≤γ\beta_L \leq \gamma), and discloses in advance the precision that test needs. Written in the coupling, the stability condition α≤αcrit\alpha \leq \alpha_{\text{crit}} reads βL≤γ\beta_L \leq \gamma, which says that a system stays correctable exactly while the leverage it takes per step does not outrun the capacity it has to correct what that leverage costs, under the conditions the registration states for Law III (Section 6.4).

The coupling of today’s systems.

No coupling has been estimated independently in the runs reported here. The original forecast of an exponent near two and its March 2026 update remain in Appendix B.5; the later error-suppression fit is inconclusive (Section 4.3). It cannot be inverted through α=1/(1−βL)\alpha=1/(1-\beta_L) to infer positive, zero or negative capability coupling. A prospective P5 comparison must identify the capability observable, estimate the ODE parameters on disjoint records, and compare its finite-window prediction with the validation trajectory under the registered precision and equivalence rules.

5.2 Quantum: additive composition

In surface code quantum error correction, each increase of two in code distance multiplies the suppression of the logical error rate by the same factor Λ\Lambda. The surface code is not concatenated: a larger distance enlarges one lattice, and syndrome extraction repeats in time, cycle by cycle, not distance by distance; the paper reads code distance as its depth variable by analogy. The gains accumulate additively (in code distance) while composing multiplicatively (in error suppression).

For the conditional common-Λ\Lambda model, first choose a reference distance d0d_0 and count added pairs of distance as n=(d−d0)/2n=(d-d_0)/2. The normalised suppression factor is f(n)=εd0/εd0+2n=Λnf(n)=\varepsilon_{d_0}/\varepsilon_{d_0+2n}=\Lambda^n when the prefactor is fixed. It satisfies f(n1+n2)=f(n1)f(n2)f(n_1+n_2)=f(n_1)f(n_2) on the admissible integer increments. A continuous exponential interpolation additionally assumes the regularity of Theorem 1(2). The measured Λ=2.14±0.02\Lambda=2.14\pm0.02 is the source’s suppression factor for each increase of two in code distance (Google Quantum AI and Collaborators 2024).

As functions of a common mathematical coordinate, an exponential with positive rate eventually exceeds any fixed power. That ordering alone does not rank quantum error correction above AI reasoning: code distance, recursive depth, observables and resource costs differ. This paper uses the quantum comparison as an analogy; Λ\Lambda is the source’s measured error-suppression factor, not a capability-growth exponent.

5.3 Physics: bounded composition

In the time crystal, the source’s linear stability analysis gives a growing antisymmetric (breathing) mode for pairs in its active region; higher-order damping, which that analysis leaves out, can stabilise the growing mode, and the pair settles into steady-state oscillation on a linearly stable limit cycle (Morrell et al. 2026).

This is bounded composition, on this paper’s reading of the system: Qr+1=min⁡(Qr+δQr,Qmax)Q_{r+1} = \min(Q_r + \delta Q_r,\, Q_{\max}). The source records only the established oscillation, so no rise toward the cycle, no ceiling and no growth exponent has been measured (Section 1.1). On the framework’s reading, a recursive channel with intrinsic losses saturates; the time crystal is consistent with that reading and does not test it.

5.4 The phase diagram

The following table separates the model premises. It is not an empirically measured phase diagram, and a value of the ODE coupling does not by itself assign a functional-equation class.
