Beside this note, the current record: Paper II’s current record, version 2.18, states that five models carried the capability arm, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek R1, Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-5.4 and Groq Qwen3, that Claude Opus 4.6 was measured only in the alignment arm, and that sequential exceeded parallel wherever both exponents could be estimated, Grok 4.1 Fast giving no parallel exponent; the table’s Claude row, its DeepSeek label and its ‘Yes’ for Grok 4.1 Fast are March 2026 entries that Paper II does not carry.

What is confirmed: (1) Sequential >> parallel universally (αseq>αpar\alpha_{\text{seq}} > \alpha_{\text{par}} for every model). (2) Power-law form fits well for Gemini 3 Flash (its row in the table above, one model’s fit and inconclusive). (3) Error reduction with compute investment is real.

What is NOT confirmed: (1) Super-linear scaling (α>1\alpha > 1) is not universal across architectures; the best fit, Gemini 3 Flash’s in the table above, is one model’s fit and inconclusive, and both of its sequential point estimates are sub-linear. (2) No universal α\alpha value exists; it varies from ∼0\sim 0 to ∼3\sim 3 depending on model and problem set. (3) The quadratic bound conjecture is neither confirmed nor refuted.

The framework should now be read as: ‘Sequential recursion yields αseq>αpar\alpha_{\text{seq}} > \alpha_{\text{par}} universally, with the magnitude of α\alpha being architecture-dependent. The key structural claim, that recursive composition produces stronger scaling than parallel composition, is confirmed. The quantitative claim that α>1\alpha > 1 for all sequential systems requires revision.’

Beside this update of March 2026, the current grading: Paper II’s current record, version 2.18, grades the sequential advantage as observed, on the evidence “Wherever both exponents could be estimated: Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably”, with no parallel exponent for Grok 4.1 Fast, and Gu et al. (2026) report the opposite direction. Version 1.104 of the theory registration (29 October 2026) records that the two arms of these runs of March 2026 were not matched in compute, and reads the runs as precursor evidence: they came before the registration and decide no proposition it registers. Every statement in this paper that the advantage is universal or confirmed is superseded by that grading.

Section 5.1, the original prediction

ARC Bound prediction (original).

Optimised large language models with explicit self-correction mechanisms will converge toward α≈2\alpha \approx 2 (β≈0.5\beta \approx 0.5). Systems with explicit critique-revise architecture will show β≈0.45\beta \approx 0.45 to 0.550.55 (α≈1.8\alpha \approx 1.8 to 2.22.2), while systems with simple chain-of-thought will show β≈0.2\beta \approx 0.2 to 0.30.3 (α≈1.25\alpha \approx 1.25 to 1.41.4). This is testable within current model generations.

Section 5.1, the version 3.1 empirical update

Version 3.1 empirical update.

The v5 experiment (6 models, 30 problems; in Paper II’s current record, version 2.18, five were measured on both arms, capability and alignment, since Claude Opus 4.6 carried the alignment arm only) does not support the original prediction. The best fit is Gemini 3 Flash’s, for which Paper II reports an endpoint sequential exponent of 0.59 with a bootstrap 95 per cent interval of minus 1.3 to 2.9, a regression sequential exponent of 0.49 with a standard error of 0.20 and a coefficient of determination of 0.86, and a parallel exponent of 0.31 by endpoint estimate; it is one model’s fit and inconclusive. Its regression exponent implies β≈−1.0\beta \approx -1.0 under α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta) instead of β≈0.5\beta \approx 0.5. That figure sits outside the [0,1)[0, 1) range Axiom 2 allows, which places the frozen regime beyond what the Bernoulli model as stated covers rather than inside it as a weak-coupling case; Paper II names it the physical regime, β<0\beta < 0. No deployed system measured to date has therefore been observed inside the regime Theorem 2 and Laws II and III, each a law under test, govern; the experimental cells of designs preregistered by timestamp are built to enter it, and the laws are predictions about that regime rather than descriptions of the one today’s systems occupy. Sub-linear scaling (α<1\alpha < 1) suggests that current AI models sit outside the coupling range the model covers (β<0\beta < 0), where accumulated context does not accelerate later steps. Two models (Grok 4.1 Fast, α≈3\alpha \approx 3; Claude Opus 4.6, α≈1.5\alpha \approx 1.5) show super-linear point estimates, but with low r2r^2 values, indicating poor power-law fits (Paper II 2.18 measured Claude Opus 4.6 in the alignment arm only; Section 4.3). The prediction that optimised systems will converge toward α≈2\alpha \approx 2 remains open but is not supported by current data. The revised empirical picture is that α\alpha is architecture-dependent, and the primary validated claim is that sequential processing yields higher α\alpha than parallel processing for every model tested (Paper II 2.18 now grades this as observed, wherever both exponents could be estimated; Section 4.3).

Section 5.4, the version 3.1 note

v3.1 note: What the v5 data points to is that current AI systems may operate in a coupling regime weaker than first assumed (β<0\beta < 0): the regression exponent of the best fit, one model’s and inconclusive (Section 4.3 prints its row whole), yields β≈−1.0\beta \approx -1.0 under the relation α=1/(1−β)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta), and the [0,1)[0, 1) range set by Axiom 2 does not admit such a value. This would place current AI systems in the diminishing-returns regime, outside the power-law regime, not deep within it as originally hypothesised.

Section 6.2, the version 3.1 note

v3.1 note: The v5 cross-architecture data shows that α\alpha varies significantly across models (∼0\sim 0 to ∼3\sim 3), consistent with different architectures having different effective β\beta values. This is consistent with the regime transition prediction, though it does not confirm it directly since the variation is across architectures rather than within a single system.

Section 6.4, the retracted initial estimate and its update of March 2026

Initial estimate (retracted): α≈2.2\alpha \approx 2.2 (n=12n = 12, 95% CI: 1.5 to 3.0). Note: this point estimate exceeded the conjectured ARC Bound of α≤2\alpha \leq 2; however, the 95% confidence interval [1.5, 3.0] was wide enough to be consistent with both the theory and its negation, and should not be treated as confirmatory of either bound violation or bound satisfaction. Update: Paper II (March 2026) extends this test to 6 frontier models with 30 problems and bootstrap confidence intervals (in its current record, version 2.18, five were measured on both arms, capability and alignment, since Claude Opus 4.6 carried the alignment arm only). The cross-architecture best fit is one model’s, Gemini 3 Flash’s, and inconclusive (Section 4.3 prints its row whole), and the bootstrap interval of its endpoint estimate contains the value two; both of its sequential point estimates, though, are well below 2, so for current systems the empirical challenge has shifted from ‘can α\alpha exceed 2?’ to ‘can α\alpha reliably exceed 1?’ Individual model point estimates range from ∼0\sim 0 (Groq Qwen3) to ∼3\sim 3 (Grok 4.1 Fast), but models with α>1\alpha > 1 have low r2r^2, suggesting poor power-law fits rather than genuine super-linear scaling. The ARC Bound conjecture is neither confirmed nor refuted by the v5 data; it remains an open conjecture that will become empirically testable if and when AI systems consistently achieve α>1\alpha > 1.

Section 7, the version 3.1 falsification status summary

Version 3.1 falsification status summary.

The v5 experiment has updated the status of three criteria: F1 (sequential advantage) is confirmed in its revised, weaker form (αseq>αpar\alpha_{\text{seq}} > \alpha_{\text{par}}, rather than α>1\alpha > 1); Paper II 2.18 now grades it as observed (Table 9). The original stronger form F1a (α>1\alpha > 1) is weakened but not definitively falsified, as two models show super-linear point estimates. F13 (alignment scaling) is refuted in its original form: αalign\alpha_{\text{align}} is not universally near zero but is architecture-dependent, with values ranging from −0.25-0.25 to +0.44+0.44 (a single unregistered run, under the caveat of Section 6.5). The falsification of F13 in its original form is an important correction: alignment scaling is a property of the architecture-training interaction, not solely of whether alignment is ‘in the loop.’ This finding motivates a revised F13 in future versions.

Section 7, the update of September 2026

Update: scope of the sequential advantage (Paper II, September 2026).

Paper II was revised on 18 September 2026 and now frames the cross-architecture replication on five analysable models of the six tested. It scopes the sequential statement to every model in which both arms were measurable, and states the parallel result as at or near zero in every model measured, with one measured exception, Gemini 3 Flash. The regression estimate on that model, its coefficient of determination and the 18 of 30 problems that entered the exponent fit are unchanged. For Gemini 3 Flash, Paper II reports an endpoint sequential exponent of 0.59 with a bootstrap 95 per cent interval of minus 1.3 to 2.9, a regression sequential exponent of 0.49 with a standard error of 0.20 and a coefficient of determination of 0.86, and a parallel exponent of 0.31 by endpoint estimate. It is one model’s fit and inconclusive. Where this paper states the sequential advantage as universal across six models, the denominator carrying it is the five in which both arms were measurable; six is the number tested. Its current record, version 2.18, counts five frontier models measured on both arms, capability and alignment, since Claude Opus 4.6 carried the alignment arm only; it grades the sequential advantage as observed wherever both exponents could be estimated (Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably), and gives the parallel exponent as near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems), and none for Grok 4.1 Fast.

Section 8, the update of March 2026

Update of March 2026, its words kept: revised empirical standing.

The v5 cross-architecture experiment (Paper II, March 2026) has tested the AI predictions against six frontier models (in Paper II’s current record, version 2.18, five were measured on both arms, capability and alignment, since Claude Opus 4.6 carried the alignment arm only). The results require an honest reassessment of what is confirmed and what requires revision:

Confirmed: (1) The sequential advantage is universal: αseq>αpar\alpha_{\text{seq}} > \alpha_{\text{par}} for every model tested. This is the framework’s core structural prediction for AI, and it holds without exception. (2) The power-law functional form fits well for at least one model (Gemini 3 Flash, whose fit is inconclusive; Section 4.3 prints its row whole), consistent with multiplicative composition. (3) Error reduction with increased sequential compute investment is real.

Beside it, the current grading: Paper II 2.18 grades the sequential advantage as observed (Section 4.3); it is neither universal nor without exception, and Gu et al. (2026) report the opposite direction. The recursive advantage named below is that observation, in one unregistered run.

Requires revision: (1) The AI scaling exponent’s best fit is one model’s and inconclusive (Section 4.3), with both sequential point estimates below one, not ≈2\approx 2. The framework predicted super-linear scaling (α>1\alpha > 1); the data shows sub-linear scaling. The key question has shifted from ‘can α\alpha exceed the quadratic bound?’ to ‘can α\alpha reliably exceed 1?’ (2) α\alpha is architecture-dependent (ranging from ∼0\sim 0 to ∼3\sim 3 across models), not universal. (3) Alignment scaling (αalign\alpha_{\text{align}}) is architecture-dependent, ranging from −0.25-0.25 to +0.44+0.44, exhibiting a three-tier hierarchy (3 positive, 2 flat, 1 negative) rather than being universally near zero, in a single unregistered run under the caveat of Section 6.5.

Open: The quadratic bound conjecture (α≤2\alpha \leq 2) is neither confirmed nor refuted. The β\beta-to-α\alpha derivation, the R*R^* crossover, and the composition operator classification remain mathematically valid but empirically untested in physical systems. The cross-domain predictions (biology, physics) are unaffected by the AI results.

The mathematical framework survives intact. What has changed is the empirical picture for AI systems: the recursive advantage is real but weaker than predicted. Whether this reflects fundamental limitations of current architectures or limitations of the experimental design (problem difficulty, compute range, measurement methodology) remains to be determined.

Appendix G.1, the note of 3 October 2026

This paper and Laws IV and V: a note of 3 October 2026, kept as printed.

Law IV is carried by proposition P15, and Law V by propositions P12 and P21. The three propositions are registered; the laws that now group them are not. This paper bears on Law V through the conditional prediction of §6.5: that alignment properties embedded within the recursive process may scale with capability, while external constraints applied post-hoc may not. Its in-loop half is untested, as criterion F13 records. Against its external half the paper reports the v5 experiment, in which the alignment exponent of six frontier models was architecture-dependent, from minus 0.25 to plus 0.44, and it records that half as refuted in its simple form. That half is a claim of the kind the registration states as P19, that external alignment does not scale with capability. The registration places P19 in no register, as a survey of current practice that motivates the genesis strategy, Law V’s register ARC-5, without being part of it, and it counts none of the seven propositions in no register as evidence for or against the survival of any law. The v5 result therefore decides nothing in Law V. The paper counts the Eden Protocol pilot of §6.5 as empirical support for the conditional implication, and states that a blind replication is still required before its results can be considered confirmatory. The pilot is a prompt-level intervention scored on matched pairs; it does not compare correction that takes part in each revision round with correction that sees only the finished output as depth rises, which P21 concerns. §3.2 argues that structural alignment must be implemented while systems remain frozen; the paper’s claim-status ladder grades as strong theoretical inference that alignment would need to be structurally load-bearing before a self-modifying system enters the super-linear regime. No run in the paper varies the order in which a system’s components are built, which P12 concerns, and nothing in it measures whether a gain installed by external post-training erodes under later capability-directed training, which P15 concerns. No result in this paper is a deciding test of P15, P12 or P21. Naming the two laws changes no result printed here: the results, their dates and their limits stand as they were.

Superseded record.

An information-theoretic heuristic (attention-based architectures). Transformer self-attention computes pairwise interactions across all NN tokens in a context window. This creates at most O(N2)O(N^2) information pathways per forward pass. Each recursive reasoning step (a chain-of-thought step) processes the accumulated context through this quadratic bottleneck. Since the information density available to each step is bounded by O(N2)O(N^2), the capability gain per step cannot exceed quadratic scaling in context length. Mapping context utilisation to the coupling parameter βL\beta_L: full quadratic utilisation corresponds to βL=0.5\beta_L = 0.5, yielding α=1/(1−0.5)=2\alpha = 1/(1-0.5) = 2. On this heuristic, Umax=I×R2U_{\max} = I \times R^2 would be an upper bound for attention-based architectures; the scope below, and corrections 2 and 4, say why it is a conjecture and not a result.

(2017) report at 20 degrees Celsius, 0.58 and 0.53 against biomass (ectomycorrhizal and marine fungi) and 0.53 against radial extension rate (saprotrophic fungi), comparisons its authors present as hypothesis generators on small data sets. It is labelled ‘consistent’ rather than ‘confirmed’ because the factors were measured at the colony level; definitive confirmation requires individual-hypha respirometry. Earlier measurement protocol, superseded in the review revision.

Earlier measurement protocol

To test the framework, we set out a standardised six-step protocol for any recursive system:

Step 1. Define one recursive cycle (one self-referential step where output becomes input).

Step 2. Measure base capability II at R=1R = 1 (no recursion). For cross-domain comparability, we operationalise II, in a working definition not yet tested and this paper’s own, outside the notation register, as the maximum rate of entropy reduction per recursive cycle, measured in bits per cycle: I=max⁡R[−ΔH/ΔR]I = \max_R [-\Delta H / \Delta R] evaluated at the first cycle (R=0R = 0 to R=1R = 1). Landauer’s principle gives the least heat for erasing a bit, kBTln⁡2k_B T \ln 2 (Landauer 1961), verified experimentally by Bérut et al. (2012); it bounds the energy cost of an irreversible step from below and does not convert energy processed into information gained, so a link from II to energy needs a model of how many bits each cycle erases. In AI, II is single-pass accuracy, without a reasoning chain (Section 4.2). In quantum error correction, II is the error reduction from one syndrome cycle. In biology, II is the metabolic efficiency gain from one branching level. U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha} is dimensionally consistent because RR is a dimensionless count.

Step 3. Measure capability UU at minimum 5 recursive depths spanning one order of magnitude. Look for the R*R^* crossover.

Step 4. Fit the candidate forms: power law (log⁡(U/I)=αlog⁡R\log(U/I) = \alpha \log R), exponential (log⁡(U/I)=λR\log(U/I) = \lambda R), logarithmic (U/I=clog⁡RU/I = c \log R) and saturating (Theorem 1, case 3). Select best fit via AIC/BIC. The power law is a prediction to test, not an assumption. This candidate set is the protocol’s own; P1 registers its rivals in full (Section 2).

Step 5. Measure βL\beta_L independently, by the linearisation method that Section 9 names as the one that recovers the relation (described in the forensic analysis listed under Code and data), not by numerical derivatives of measured gains, which Section 9 found biased towards βL≈0.95\beta_L \approx 0.95 whatever the true value. Compare the exponent the measured βL\beta_L implies with the fitted exponent, reading 1/(1−βL)1/(1-\beta_L) over the measured window as the complete solution of Axiom 2 gives it, under the margin of 0.10 that P5 registers for that comparison.

Step 6. Report α\alpha with 95% confidence intervals. Submit to public repository.

What the classification settles is the behaviour of the three composition rules set out above. This axiom captures the essential feature of recursive processing: each step’s marginal amplification depends on accumulated amplification. When βL=0\beta_L = 0, steps are independent and amplification grows linearly. When βL>0\beta_L > 0, accumulated amplification accelerates future gains (super-linear scaling). The parameter βL\beta_L measures how much of accumulated context each new step can effectively leverage. Operating on the amplification factor gg rather than on absolute capability Q=I⋅gQ = I \cdot g preserves the separability asserted in Axiom 1: the amplification function depends only on recursive depth, not on base potential.

What it does not show is that any real system satisfies the axioms: the βL\beta_L-to-α\alpha relation, the crossover and the classification are untested in physical systems, the AI exponent’s best fit is one model’s and inconclusive, no exponent has been measured in a time crystal, and the ARC Bound, registered as a ceiling of at most two for same-class correctors, is untested, its point value two a conjecture. The table below sets what the paper does not claim beside what it does.

The runs of March 2026 are precursor evidence that decides no registered proposition (Section 4.3): the sequential advantage was observed only where both exponents could be estimated, and Gu et al. (2026) report the opposite direction; the one interpretable capability fit is inconclusive and below one; and the alignment run cannot decide criterion F13 (Section 6.5). B.12 Further passages of version 5.21, retained as superseded wording

The following passages of version 5.21 are retained as printed, as superseded wording. Each note names the correction and where the current statement stands; none is restored as a current claim, and no registered text or study result changes.

Superseded passage 20.

The abstract of version 5.21, as printed. The present abstract states the contribution and the evidence at their corrected scope; the question of lost control with which it opened stands in Section 1.

I believe advanced AI is an existential risk unless values and correction are built into how it reasons; only proof will move the world. If control of a capable AI system were lost and could not be won back, what the system itself carries would decide what it does. This paper asks whether recursion amplifies capability in the same way across very different fields, so that a self-improving system’s growth could be predicted before it scales. Between 2024 and 2026, programmes in AI reasoning, quantum error correction, acoustic physics and consciousness science reported results that bear on recursive or recurrent processing, in different forms. We formalise the question with three axioms (separability, cumulative advantage, continuity) and a recursive composition operator. Under each case’s hypotheses, Cauchy’s functional equations give multiplicative composition a power law and additive composition an exponential; capped composition stays bounded. Inside the model the asymptotic exponent is derived, not fitted: α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) for coupling βL\beta_L; base potential and depth must interact multiplicatively; and a crossover depth R*=α/aR^* = \alpha/a, independent of base potential, separates approximately linear from compounding gains. Five structural properties follow, two on premises added to the axioms. The ARC Bound is stated as registered: the ceiling of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, is at most two for same-class correctors, and the point value two is a conjecture. The evidence is graded: the AI exponent’s one interpretable fit is inconclusive, the time crystal is an analogy with no exponent measured, and the neuroscience mapping is structural. Thirteen falsification criteria and a cross-domain forward prediction are stated; a computational suite checks the closed forms but tests no real system. Each result holds inside its stated model.

Superseded passage 21.

The first paragraph of the introduction of version 5.21, as printed. Its inference that a frozen system’s scaling is predictable, so that structural alignment is to be built while systems remain frozen, is withdrawn: neither frozen weights nor a fixed update rule fixes an exponent (Section 3.2). The question and the programme’s position stand in Section 1.

I believe advanced AI is an existential risk unless values and correction are built into how it reasons; only proof will move the world. If control of a capable AI system were lost and could not be won back, what the system itself carries would decide what it does. The programme’s position is that people keep oversight, containment and shutdown for as long as they physically can, and never give them up by choice; correction built into a system is the contingency for control lost against our will, not a reason to let go of it. If the way a recursive process combines its gains fixes how its capability grows with depth, then the scaling of a self-improving system could be predicted from a property measured before it scales: if you can measure the composition operator in a new system, you can predict its scaling function before measuring the full scaling curve (Section 3.2). On that reading, structural alignment (embedding values within the composition operator itself; the values are for international consensus, Section 6.5) is to be built while systems remain frozen and their scaling is predictable, and judged on whether it keeps a system useful as well as safe. This paper asks whether recursion amplifies capability in the same way across very different fields: is the pattern that separate research programmes have reported (Section 1.1) a coincidence, or are we observing different expressions of a single structural principle?

Superseded passage 22.

The statement of the claim in the introduction of version 5.21, as printed. That a measurable composition operator determines a system’s scaling function is withdrawn as a general inference: an equation on the observable, not associativity of an update rule, constrains the family (Theorem 1). Its conditional statement on substrates stands in Section 1.

We argue that the pattern reflects a principle, but not the one that might be expected. We do not claim that one equation fits all domains. We claim something more specific: that, for any recursive system that satisfies the axioms, a measurable property (its composition operator) determines its scaling function, and that five qualitative properties follow from the recursive architecture, two of them on premises added to the axioms (Theorem 4). The mathematical form differs across domains because the composition operator differs. The structural properties hold in every substrate whose recursion satisfies the axioms, because the axioms name no substrate.

Superseded passage 23.

The related-work paragraph of version 5.21, as printed. Stability results are specific to their equations and do not transfer to noisy finite data (Section 3.2); the renormalisation-group comparison is an analogy (Superseded passage 27).

Functional equations and their stability.

The classification of Theorem 1 rests on Cauchy’s functional equations (Cauchy 1821); that a function approximately satisfying one of them lies near an exact solution of the same equation is the stability theorem of Hyers and Ulam (Hyers 1941; Ulam 1960). The renormalisation-group parallel of Section 3.2 draws on Kadanoff’s scaling picture for Ising models near the critical point (Kadanoff 1966) and on Wilson’s renormalisation group (Wilson 1971).

Superseded passage 24.

Frozen models and self-modification in version 5.21, as printed. A fixed update rule does not imply a sub-linear exponent, frozen weights do not fix an agent, and the two-regime reading and its inference for the timing of alignment are withdrawn as general claims. The hypothesis now stated is that specified changes to an improvement procedure alter later gains under controlled resources (Section 3.2). The estimate of about 2.2 stays retracted. People keep oversight, containment and shutdown for as long as they can be held; embedded correction is the contingency for control lost against our will.

Frozen models versus recursive self-modification: two distinct regimes.

A critical application of this classification concerns the distinction between current AI systems and hypothetical self-modifying ones. Current frontier AI models are frozen during inference: when they generate extended reasoning chains, the underlying weights, and with them the composition rule, remain fixed (attention patterns still vary with the input). The composition operator ⊕\oplus does not change between steps. This architectural constraint confines such systems to multiplicative composition through a finite-dimensional parameter space, producing power-law fits with exponents below one, which Paper II names the physical regime, α<1\alpha < 1 (Section 5.1). Empirically, Paper II’s estimate of the exponent rests on one model, Gemini 3 Flash, and is inconclusive, with both sequential point estimates below one (Section 4.3 prints its row whole). Such a fit does not by itself place the model outside Axiom 2: α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) is the asymptotic exponent of the axiom’s solution, and over a finite window, below the crossover depth of Theorem 3, that solution can return a fitted exponent below one for a positive coupling.

The Cauchy classification reveals precisely why. In a frozen system the same fixed operator composes every reasoning step, and with α<1\alpha < 1 the resulting gains are real but diminishing. By contrast, a system capable of recursive self-modification, one that rewrites its own composition function ⊕\oplus during operation, would occupy a qualitatively different position in the classification. If step rr improves the operator used at step r+1r+1, the self-referential coupling βL\beta_L would, on this model, be positive and could rise, yielding α=1/(1−βL)>1\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) > 1. This transition does not require quantum hardware or additive composition; it requires only that the system can modify its own reasoning architecture during inference.

No current AI system achieves this. Earlier versions of this paper did predict super-linear scaling (α>1\alpha > 1) for current, frozen models (the original ARC Bound prediction, “testable within current model generations”, now kept in Appendix B.5), and that prediction was not borne out; the estimate of about 2.2 is retracted (Section 4.3). On the present reading, super-linear scaling belongs to a regime that does not yet exist. The practical consequence, previewed in Section 1, is that structural alignment is to be built while systems remain frozen and their scaling is predictable, and judged beside a measure of usefulness, as every safety measure is (Section 6.5). Once self-modification arrives, the composition operator becomes a moving target, and on this model a fixed external safeguard would fall behind a capability that compounds. Correction built into the operator is the contingency for control lost against our will; oversight, containment and shutdown stay in human hands for as long as they can be held. Guaranteed controllability after self-modification is not an established result of this programme.

Superseded passage 25.

The account of Assumption 3 in version 5.21, as printed. The stability results of Hyers and of Baker and colleagues are global statements about the stated equations; they do not make a noisy finite sample stable, or evidence for a scaling family (Section 3.2).

Assumption 3 is particularly significant for the framework’s applicability. The Hyers-Ulam stability theorem (Hyers 1941; Ulam 1960) proves that any function approximately satisfying one of Cauchy’s functional equations must lie close to an exact solution of that same equation. Formally, for the additive equation, if |f(x+y)−f(x)−f(y)|≤ε|f(x + y) - f(x) - f(y)| \leq \varepsilon for all x,yx, y, there is an exact additive gg with |f(x)−g(x)|≤ε|f(x) - g(x)| \leq \varepsilon (Hyers 1941); for the exponential equation, and so for the multiplicative one by a change of variables, the result is superstability: a real function on a vector space with |f(x+y)−f(x)f(y)|≤ε|f(x + y) - f(x) f(y)| \leq \varepsilon for all x,yx, y is either bounded or an exact solution (Baker et al. 1979). Real systems never satisfy the axioms exactly: biological networks are noisy, AI reasoning chains have variable quality, quantum error correction operates with imperfect gates. Within each equation, the corresponding form is therefore stable under perturbation. The earlier phrasing that made the three forms “stable attractors in function space” is withdrawn, because a function that satisfies none of the equations is not drawn toward any of them; the stability is per-equation, not a partition of function space. Whether power laws, exponentials, or logarithmic forms are empirically ubiquitous in nature is a separate question about how often systems approximately satisfy one of these equations in the first place, and Hyers-Ulam does not by itself settle it.

Superseded passage 26.

The structural implication of version 5.21, as printed. A stability theorem does not make an empirical scaling law mathematically compelled; within Axiom 2 the exponent follows from the coupling only under the model’s premises. Measuring the operator yields a prediction only when its description is justified without the validation curve and sealed in advance (Section 3.2); the forward prediction as printed is Superseded passage 1.

Structural implication: per-equation stability.

Combining Theorem 1 (Cauchy 1821), the Hyers-Ulam stability theorem (Hyers 1941), and Theorem 2 (α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L)): once a system is known to approximately satisfy one of Cauchy’s equations, its scaling form is not a free parameter to be fitted or evolved. It is mathematically compelled by the composition operator, and within the power-law form the exponent is compelled by the self-referential coupling βL\beta_L. Each of the recognised scaling forms is per-equation stable: a small perturbation of an exact solution stays near an exact solution of the same equation (Hyers 1941; Baker et al. 1979). The distinction matters: ‘Why is this system’s exponent 2?’ has two kinds of answer. The mechanistic answer describes the coupling. The mathematical answer says: no other value is possible for this composition operator with this coupling strength.

This has a crucial implication: if you can measure ⊕\oplus in a new system, you can predict its scaling function before measuring the full scaling curve. This is the framework’s strongest cross-domain prediction (Section 6.1).

Superseded passage 27.

The renormalisation-group comparison and the quadratic limit in version 5.21, as printed. The comparison is an analogy, not a derivation. That relevant operators grow and irrelevant ones shrink under the flow, and that a critical fixed point’s exponents follow from its universality class, are standard results of the renormalisation group (Kadanoff 1966; Wilson 1971); that a system which changed its own class would scale without bound is this paper’s conjecture, with no prediction or test registered or planned, and no theorem here shows that a change of operator causes unbounded growth. Law III’s value rests on its registered premises (Section 6.4), and frozen and changing architectures must both be measured.

On this model, a system that modifies its own composition operator changes the scaling exponent itself; the passage from bounded to unbounded α\alpha is not a smooth acceleration within one operator. This has a structural parallel in the renormalisation group in physics (Wilson 1971), where relevant operators grow under RG flow and irrelevant operators shrink. At a critical fixed point, the scaling exponent is determined by the system’s universality class (its dimensionality and symmetry). But if a system could change its own universality class during the flow, the fixed-point structure would collapse and the system would exhibit unbounded scaling until it settled into a new class. As an analogy, not a derivation: a self-modifying AI system would resemble a physical system that rewrites its own Hamiltonian, escaping the fixed-point constraints that a fixed composition operator imposes.

If there is a ‘quadratic limit’ (α≤2\alpha \leq 2), it is not a Cauchy prediction. The value two comes from the pacing derivation of Law III, the ARC Ceiling, a law under test, at γ=1/2\gamma = 1/2 (Section 6.4; correction 9). The count of O(N2)O(N^2) pairwise attention pathways in a fixed transformer is a heuristic for why frozen architectures fall below it and proves nothing about capability (corrections 2 and 4). A self-modifying system that expands its own representational capacity at each step would not face that count, and the mathematics sets no upper bound on α\alpha: the Cauchy framework does not forbid an exponent above two, and it does not predict one.

Superseded passage 28.

The crossover depth in version 5.21, as printed. R*R^* is a characteristic scale at which the local elasticity reaches half its limiting value, not the onset of super-linear growth (Theorem 3); it is free of II only while aa and βL\beta_L stay fixed, and other shifted growth models have characteristic scales too. The literature search of 12 August 2026 is retained as the dated record of what that search found, not as a present novelty claim.

R*R^* is the crossover depth: the recursive depth at which compounding overtakes linear gains. Below R*R^*, additional recursion provides approximately constant marginal benefit. Above R*R^*, returns compound and capability grows super-linearly.

Critically, R*R^* is a derived quantity. It depends on measurable parameters (α\alpha and aa) and is not a free parameter to be fitted. This provides an independent consistency check: measure α\alpha and aa separately, compute the predicted R*R^*, and verify that the observed crossover matches. Since R*R^* depends only on the scaling exponent and rate constant (not on base potential II), the crossover depth is a property of the recursive architecture itself, not of the input quality.

The existence of R*R^* is, to this programme’s knowledge, absent in this form from other scaling frameworks: crossover scales do turn up elsewhere (logistic growth, renormalisation-group crossovers), but what is predicted here is a crossover sited at R*=α/aR^* = \alpha/a, pinned by two parameters each of which can be measured on its own (a literature search of 12 August 2026, cross-checked against two years of repository reports; negative findings have the status of not-found-by-that-search, never does-not-exist). It distinguishes recursive amplification from simple redundancy: redundant systems show uniform (typically logarithmic) improvement with repetition; recursive systems show a qualitative transition at a specific, predictable depth.

These results refine, rather than refute, the hypothesis. The sequential advantage appears to have boundary conditions: it holds within task-appropriate depth ranges, for convergent problems, and breaks down at extreme depths or for divergent tasks. Superseded passage 32.

Chain-of-thought composition in version 5.21, as printed. That a later step uses earlier reasoning establishes neither the multiplicative equation nor the cumulative-advantage law; the proposed model is tested by an independent estimate of βL\beta_L and a held-out trajectory (Section 5.1).

In chain-of-thought reasoning, each step builds hierarchically on accumulated insight. Step r+1r+1 does not merely add new information; it restructures the problem representation using everything accumulated through step rr. This is multiplicative composition: the gain at each step depends on the quality of the accumulated representation, less than proportionally (were it strictly proportional, growth would be exponential).

Superseded passage 33.

The completeness statement of version 5.21, as printed. Theorem 1 does not show that every associative recursion induces one of its equations, or that its families exhaust classical scaling, and stability does not transfer automatically (Section 5.4). The cosmological reading to which it points stays at the close (Section 10): the mathematics does not deny it, and it is a reason for nothing else.

Structural implication: the completeness of classical scaling.

Since, under Theorem 1’s hypotheses (associativity, continuity and the stated scalar-composition scoping), a recursive process combines its steps through one of the three composition operators, and since the Hyers-Ulam theorem guarantees stability under perturbation, the space of classical scaling behaviours under those hypotheses is low-dimensional: a choice of form (power law, exponential, saturation, or the linear and logarithmic Cauchy solutions), a coefficient, and an exponent or rate. This completeness statement follows from Theorem 1 and the Hyers-Ulam theorem under their hypotheses; it is not a separate theorem. On this reading, the phase diagram above, originally motivated by AI systems, is a cross-section of a wider diagram for the classical recursive systems that satisfy those hypotheses; the companion paper, Eastwood (2026r), develops the cross-domain connection, and the cosmological reading stands, as conjecture, at the close (Section 10).

The conservation or optimisation constraint takes a different form in each derivation (energy minimisation in West, supply-demand balance in Banavar, steady-state energy balance in Demetrius); together with multiplicative composition and space-filling it suffices for d/(d+1)d/(d+1).

Physics instances. The formula α=d/(d+1)\alpha = d/(d+1) is not restricted to biology. It appears wherever a dd-dimensional hierarchical network, subject to a conservation or optimisation constraint on resource flow, partitions a (d+1)(d+1)-dimensional space. The formula matches known or reference exponents in several physics domains:

These four instances carry no aggregate error figure. The sub-0.2 per cent mean quoted earlier was withdrawn on 14 August 2026 (correction 10), since averaging over analytic identities is no measure of predictive accuracy, and the earthquake B-value row went the same day (correction 11), being a definitional identity kept only as a variable-pair case study. Nothing in this set is biological: the subjects are rocks, crystal surfaces in growth, and phase transitions. Yet the same formula matches them: two by analytic identity, and two against reference values without a named source. In each case the physical system contains a hierarchical branching network of dimension dd subject to a conservation constraint: a KPZ growth front divides 2D space along a 1D network; a percolation cluster takes the form of a 2D fractal; a propagating crack cuts branching networks through the material. The formula has clear failures where this network structure or conservation condition is absent (Ising model, polymer scaling, galaxy clustering), clarifying its domain of applicability: α=d/(d+1)\alpha = d/(d+1) applies wherever a dd-dimensional hierarchical network, subject to conservation or optimisation of resource flow, optimally partitions a (d+1)(d+1)-dimensional space.

Superseded passage 36.

The conclusion of version 5.21 before its conjectural extrapolation, as printed. The crossover is a smooth characteristic scale, not a critical depth or threshold (Theorem 3); invariance across input qualities needs fixed parameters; the composition description predicts only when it is justified independently of the validation curve; and the statement that the programme had not located these predictions in a single-domain theory records that date’s search, not a present priority claim. The observation on the systems discussed and the closing hypothesis stand in Section 10 at their corrected status.

Every system discussed in this paper (silicon neural networks, superconducting qubits, millimetre polymer beads, cortical neural circuits) maintains a low-entropy state far from equilibrium and, on this paper’s reading, feeds its outputs back into its inputs. The framework predicts that below a critical depth the gains are ordinary and above it they compound, with the transition universal in structure and domain-specific in form; no such depth has yet been measured in any of them (criterion F7), and a claim that the transition is sharp would need a criterion of its own.

We have formalised this observation. The composition operator ⊕\oplus sorts recursive systems by the functional equation their scaling satisfies: under the stated hypotheses it determines the functional form of scaling from measurable algebraic properties. The five derived properties (threshold, depth-dependence, base-quality dependence, multiplicative interaction, regime boundaries) follow as theorems from three axioms and, for two of them, the premises Theorem 4 names, not as empirical generalisations.

The framework issues predictions that the programme has been unable to locate in any theory confined to a single domain. It predicts the scaling behaviour of new recursive systems from their composition operator alone. It predicts a scaling crossover at a derived depth R*R^* that is independent of base quality and consistent across input qualities for a given architecture. It predicts that a measured βL\beta_L determines α\alpha via α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L), a relationship proved for the axiom’s solutions and checked numerically to R2=1.00000000R^2 = 1.00000000; the blind test of Section 9 neither supports nor refutes it for other systems. It states the ARC Bound as the theory registration holds it, a ceiling of at most two for correctors of the system’s own class, which needs P6 and P20 and nothing else, with the point value two a conjecture. Its own earlier form, the coupling at which the sustained exponent reaches two (βL=0.5\beta_L = 0.5, α=2\alpha = 2), is an early-framework conjecture that decides nothing registered (criteria F5 and F11), with the O(N2)O(N^2) tally of self-attention pathways only a heuristic for the frozen regime; on that conjecture two is a scaling limit, not a speed limit, which systems can exceed in transient supercritical excursions without staying stably self-correcting. And it conjectures that bounded systems exhibit composition operator transitions that could explain why different studies of the same system can observe different scaling regimes (Conjecture 5). These predictions and conjectures are specific, falsifiable, and forward-looking.

If the predictions fail, we will have learned where the structural analogy breaks down. If they hold, we will have identified a principle that connects intelligence, computation, and the physics of order across substrates.

Intelligence may not be a property of particular materials. It may be what happens on the far side of the recursive threshold.

E A prospective measurement protocol

This protocol asks whether composition predicts fresh observations better than rival models. It is a prospective design proposal. Existing registrations retain their own definitions, margins and rules.

Step 1: fix the system and quantity. Name the observable, its units, the population of tasks or physical states, the depth origin and the resource budget. State whether weights, code, memory, prompts or tools may change. Define usable performance and any error burden separately. A common letter does not make accuracy, metabolic rate and physical error suppression commensurable.

Step 2: measure the baseline and justify composition. Measure II at the declared first pass in the same units as UU. Specify how a composition class or parameter is assigned before inspecting the validation trajectory. Use mechanistic evidence, independent observers blinded to the answer where appropriate, or an expressly separated calibration sample. Record the rule, exclusions and uncertainty; an assignment inferred from the observed exponent is not a prediction.

Step 3: lock the prediction. From that information, specify the candidate family, the parameter prediction and interval, and an operational crossover if one is claimed. Freeze the held-out data split, resource controls, measurement schedule and analysis before validation. Parameter estimates and validation outcomes must come from disjoint records or a sealed early-window/later-window design. A transform of the same fitted curve is an internal check, not independent confirmation.

Step 4: establish what the design can distinguish. Size and place the observations by a design analysis that reports its sensitivity to the named alternatives, noise, saturation and dependence. A small depth ladder is not automatically decisive. Predetermine the tolerances, multiplicity treatment, failure conditions and inconclusive outcomes. A post-hoc change of domain or effective dimension cannot rescue a failed prediction.

Step 5: compare adequate rivals on a common response. Include the exact power, the shifted cumulative-advantage solution, exponential, logarithmic, saturating and broken-power candidates where justified. Respect the baseline: for example g(R)=eλ(R−1)g(R)=e^{\lambda(R-1)} and g(R)=1+clog⁡Rg(R)=1+c\log R satisfy g(1)=1g(1)=1; unshifted versions need not. Prespecify observation-error models and comparable likelihoods, including transformation Jacobians where required, before using information criteria (Xiao et al. 2011). Evaluate held-out prediction as well as fit. For a claimed mechanism, specify an intervention that distinguishes it from a descriptive curve with the same shape.

Step 6: report the whole test. Publish the locked prediction, code version, inclusion record, observations, uncertainty and all deviations. Report supported, refuted or inconclusive only under the registered rule. A failed predictive test is evidence about that prediction even when a later diagnostic identifies misspecification; the diagnostic motivates a new test and does not turn failure into support.

The earlier six-step protocol is retained in Appendix B. Its proposed common entropy unit was not validated, and its bare curve-selection instructions did not specify an observation-error model. This revision makes neither a new data analysis nor a change to a study already registered.

F Computational validation suite

This appendix summarises the computational checks of Theorems 1 to 4 and of Conjecture 5. The scripts and results deposited for them are listed under Code and data, after the conclusion; the count of Appendix F.1 and the crossover figures of Appendices F.4 and F.8 stand there at most in a printed summary, without the computation behind them. Tests were conducted using Python 3.12 with NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib.

F.1 Theorem 1 validation (Cauchy classification)

Fifteen systems were tested across three composition regimes (5 multiplicative, 5 additive, 5 bounded). Each system was evaluated on whether its measured composition rule matched the predicted scaling function.

Result: 15/15 correct classifications (100%). No system was misclassified. The classification itself is proved (Appendix A.1); the check confirms only that each system, built in a known regime, was assigned the form of that regime.

F.2 Theorem 2 validation (βL→α\beta_L \to \alpha identity)

The relationship α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) was tested against 30 exact Bernoulli ODE solutions with βL\beta_L spanning 0.05 to 0.92. For each test case, βL\beta_L was measured blindly from the marginal gain structure (dg/dRdg/dR vs gg in log-log space), α\alpha was predicted, and the predicted value was compared against the true scaling exponent.

Result: R2=1.00000000R^2 = 1.00000000 (eight decimal places). Regression slope: 1.000102. Mean absolute error: 0.002%. This agrees with the closed form to numerical precision; that α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L) is exact is proved in Appendix A.2.

F.3 Theorem 2a validation (non-additivity)

The non-additivity proof was verified numerically. For multiple (I1,I2,R1,R2)(I_1, I_2, R_1, R_2) combinations across all βL∈(0,1)\beta_L \in (0,1): if UU were additive (U=f(I)+h(R)U = f(I) + h(R)), then U(I1,R1)−U(I1,R2)U(I_1, R_1) - U(I_1, R_2) would equal U(I2,R1)−U(I2,R2)U(I_2, R_1) - U(I_2, R_2). For distinct base values and depths with different amplification, the product model makes those differences unequal. This checks a consequence of the assumed product form; it does not establish that form empirically.

Scope of the recorded check. The reported numerical examples concern non-additivity under a product model. They do not prove the earlier universal claim for S=U(I,R)/[I+((1−βL)aR)α]S=U(I,R)/[I+((1-\beta_L)aR)^\alpha], which is withdrawn. With βL=1/2\beta_L=1/2, a=2a=2, I=1/4I=1/4 and R=2R=2, the compatible exact solution is g(R)=R2g(R)=R^2, so S=4/17<1S=4/17<1. The ratio also requires a defined normalisation before its denominator is physically interpretable. The non-additivity theorem follows from varying II and a non-constant gg on a product domain, not from S>1S>1.

F.4 Theorem 3 validation (R*R^* crossover)

The crossover depth R*=1/[(1−βL)a]=α/aR^* = 1/[(1-\beta_L)a] = \alpha/a was tested by comparing the predicted crossover with the numerically measured transition point (where ρ=1\rho = 1).

Historical report, not usable validation. Earlier versions printed a 2 to 7% error and an input-quality invariance result here, and a 62% mean error in Appendix F.8. Their definitions and underlying computations are not recoverable from the deposited scripts. Neither figure carries evidential weight. The characteristic-scale identity is proved analytically; an empirical crossover requires the prospective operational definition in Section 6.3. Holding aa and βL\beta_L fixed makes the algebra independent of II, but does not test whether a real change of input quality preserves those parameters.

F.5 Theorem 4 validation (five properties)

Ten recursive systems and five non-recursive controls were scored on the five derived properties. Recursive systems scored a mean of 4.2/5; non-recursive controls scored 2.8/5. The difference (Δ=1.4\Delta = 1.4) is consistent with the framework’s prediction but the sample size yields p=0.095p = 0.095, which does not reach conventional significance. (In plain English: the result goes in the predicted direction, recursive systems do score higher, but with only 15 total samples, a difference at least this large would arise about one time in ten even if there were no true effect. Scientists typically require one in twenty or better. More data is needed.)

Result: Direction correct; statistical power insufficient for definitive confirmation. Larger samples are required.

F.6 Conjecture 5 validation (⊕\oplus phase transitions)

Four systems were tested for depth-dependent composition transitions: (1) exact Bernoulli ODE (control), (2) logistic growth, (3) gradient descent with momentum, (4) Kuramoto oscillators.

Results: The Bernoulli control maintained constant βL\beta_L (σ<10−6\sigma < 10^{-6}). All three bounded systems showed systematic βL\beta_L transitions: logistic growth from βL≈0.5\beta_L \approx 0.5 (growth phase) to βL→−∞\beta_L \to -\infty (saturation), gradient descent from βL≈0.52\beta_L \approx 0.52 (exploration) to βL≈0.98\beta_L \approx 0.98 (convergence), Kuramoto oscillators from βL≈1.7\beta_L \approx 1.7 (growth) to βL≈20\beta_L \approx 20 (saturation). Transitions appeared in all three bounded systems tested and not in the unbounded Bernoulli control.

F.7 Negative controls

Four non-recursive systems were tested: (1) Gaussian noise, (2) linear decay, (3) sinusoidal oscillation, (4) random walk. None produced false positive signals (S>1S > 1 or α>1\alpha > 1).

Recorded result: none of the four chosen controls triggered the stated indicators. This small constructed set does not establish a general false-positive rate or a classifier of every recursive process.

F.8 Failures and boundary cases

Two results fell short of expectations:

R*R^* absolute value: The historical 62% figure and the 2 to 7% figure above remain unresolved and are not evidence for or against a stated crossover prediction. The deposited summary does not expose a common definition or the computations needed to reconcile them. Their original wording is preserved in Appendix B; a fresh calculation must be identified as new work, never as recovery of the original.

Newton’s method: Local convergence near roots yields βL>1.0\beta_L > 1.0 (quadratic convergence), which falls outside the framework’s domain βL∈[0,1)\beta_L \in [0, 1). The framework correctly identifies this as a boundary case where the Bernoulli ODE model does not apply.

These failures are reported for completeness and scientific integrity. They bound the framework’s applicability and inform future refinement.

G The paper’s place in the ARC Theory

G.1 The five laws and this paper

The five laws, and this paper’s place among them. The ARC Theory is carried by five numbered laws. Laws I to III, registered on 8 September 2026, are the three set out below: each is a conjectured invariant relation under test, each is graded separately, and each carries its own kill condition; Law III is registered as a conditional specialisation of Law II, so it is not called supported while Law II stands refuted, and a result on it is never independent corroboration of Law II. Laws IV and V, the ARC Persistence Law and the ARC Embedding Law, were added on 24 September 2026 and registered as laws on 15 October 2026 (version 1.103), each a law under test: Law IV has not yet been tested, and the registered result on Law V’s placement limb is given in Section 8. Their mathematics is still being developed (Laws IV and V: the mathematics, version 1.2, 29 October 2026), and the note of 3 October 2026 that placed this paper against them is kept in Appendix B.5.

First Law · The ARC Principle. Its equation, the ARC Equation, is U=I×RαU = I \times R^{\alpha}. Recursion converts into capability at a measured exponent. Second Law · The ARC Co-Scaling Law. βC>k\beta_C > k (βC\beta_C is the correction exponent, not the coupling βL\beta_L carried through this paper). Correction has the asymptotic scaling advantage where its exponent exceeds the drift exponent, burden has it where the correction exponent is the smaller, and at equality coefficients, delay, backlog and saturation decide the outcome, as version 1.104 of the theory registration states the law (carried by its proposition P4). Third Law · The ARC Ceiling. αcrit=1/(1−γ)\alpha_{\text{crit}} = 1/(1-\gamma). The most a self-correcting system can grow is set by its corrector’s shortfall; the ARC Bound is the registered claim that this ceiling is at most two for same-class correctors, its point value two a conjecture.

The ARC Principle names the first of those three, the founding identity, and the five laws together are the five ARC Laws. This paper is none of the three. It is the cross-domain foundation of Law I and the formalism of the growth exponent that Law III caps: the axioms, the theorems and the proofs from which the scaling exponent, the classification of functional forms and the crossover depth are derived, with the cross-domain evidence for the exponent and the falsification table for the framework. Laws II and III are stated here as registered, and their derivations are other papers’: Paper X carries the Second Law’s theorem, and the founding paper and the statement paper, which carries the theory and its current status, set out the theory’s laws. Paper I states Law I formally and gives a preliminary result for it. Read this one for the mathematics of the exponent and its forms.

Under version 1.104, Law IV has two limbs: its retention limb is the registered claim of proposition P15, word for word, and its comparison limb has no registered proposition yet; Law V carries propositions P12 and P21.

G.2 Its position in the theory

Its position inside the theory is the mathematical foundation on which the result papers and frame papers depend. The trials that would decide Law I’s registered propositions are drafted and not yet registered (Section 8 gives the registered trials and their status); the working-paper status of this document reflects that stage. Section 2 compares the work with prior work.
